en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fuyuan Shiwu Gong:

In the past, when Great Master Bodhidharma sat in wall-contemplation at Shaolin, he transmitted the mind through a single word alone, silently revealing the true essence so that people might realize it for themselves;
he originally had no manifold explanations. Therefore, the Second Patriarch possessed innate wisdom from his youth and was exceptionally enlightened. Thus...
At the time of the secret transmission, [Shenxiu] directly realized its subtlety and said, "It is clearly and eternally known; words cannot reach it.
Bodhidharma first certified this, saying, "This is precisely the intrinsically pure mind; do not harbor further doubts.
Thereafter, for four generations, they transmitted it through silent realization of its essence without speaking of it openly. It was only upon reaching Chan Master Heze Shenhui that...

Dharma recorded a prophecy concerning a "suspended thread," fearing that the essence of the school might perish. He therefore explicitly taught the single word "knowing" as the gateway to all wonders.
By this means, the substance of the true mind was revealed to the world; those who secretly conformed to and intimately realized it were not few.
Nevertheless, the knowing of this mind is empty, luminous, and quiescently illuminating; its nature is inherently spiritual and intuitive.
It is not the kind of cognition that the world calls "relying on objects and depending on conditions" that constitutes its essence.

Since the Tang dynasty, the various patriarchs have transmitted this [teaching] to one another, branching into schools and sects. Whether it be the practice of striking with staffs or shouting "Ho," or even brandishing pitchforks, dancing with ritual tablets, drawing bows, or rolling balls—each established its own mysterious gate, and their methods of transformation were diverse;
yet when one investigates their great capacity and great function, they are none other than the direct manifestation of the mind.
The subtlety of the essence reaches a point where it cannot help but manifest through such expressions as "ascending the hall," "entering the room," and "instructing the assembly.
Observing their vigorous exhortations and guiding instructions, one sees they were all spoken extemporaneously, direct and without concealment.

Beginning with the masters of the Southern Song dynasty and thereafter, there was a gradual tendency toward composing chapters and crafting phrases, which degenerated into artificial fabrication; there even emerged discourses characterized by brevity, clumsiness, novelty, and artifice.
This causes those who study speech to become groundless and unexamined, leading them to perpetuate these errors one after another, which is deeply shameful to those of true discernment.
Little do they realize that the Way of Direct Pointing transmits mind-to-mind and must necessarily be self-realized; as soon as it involves verbal explanation, it becomes the secondary meaning.

How much more so for those who strive to engage in artificial creation? Whenever I have discussed this with scholars who have attained mastery of the school, I have never failed to sigh deeply on their behalf.
Master Gong of Shiwu, who resides at Fuyuan Hermitage, early on received the transmission from Jie’an.

Having dwelt in the mountains for over thirty years, he entered meditative concentration to contemplate the mind and attained a wondrous realization of the true essence. Therefore, his words—*not...* [text fragment]...are not [artificial].
This is a creative work that flows forth spontaneously from the very core of his being. Reading his various verses on mountain dwelling, one perceives a distinct legacy of the style of Hanshanzi.
Furthermore, his words for formal sermons and instructions to the assembly are all direct, earnest, and profoundly accurate;

they are truly capable of awakening and inspiring those who encounter them. How could those who merely study the words ever be able to imitate them through the superficial workings of their conscious intellect?
Alas! It is an autumn when the ancient Way has been overturned by waves of disorder, and heterodox doctrines are flourishing.
Throughout the vast and desolate universe, no author of such works is heard of. Who could be raised from the Pure Abode of Silent Radiance to discuss this matter together?
Preface by the Śramaṇa Lái Fù of Yǎngjìng Línyǐn Chán Monastery, written in the third month of spring in the year of Rénxū,
the fifteenth year of the Hongwǔ era.
I have heard it said that the Buddha-way does not reside in words and letters; yet how could it be complete apart from words and letters?

Sentient beings are unable to realize Buddhahood, and the Buddhas never discriminate among sentient beings. Thus, the Buddha enters into sentient beings without their being aware of it, and sentient beings reach the state of Buddhahood without practicing toward it.

Therefore it is said: "In a single pit there is no difference in the soil; the source and the stream are one and the same water. This is like the analogy of wind and water interacting with one another.
Casting [the hook], they meet by chance without prior appointment. Water has no waves without wind; wind has no surges without water.
The essence of wind is fundamentally formless, yet it forms patterns upon entering the water. When the pond water is settled, still, and level, it stirs and surges upon meeting the wind.

Yet, water and wind do not interact with one another. Where, then, do the characteristics of motion and stillness reside? This directly reveals the Dharma-gate of non-duality: that sentient beings and Buddhas ultimately return to oneness.

The substance [of the teaching] enters into the Perfect School (Yuanzong); only then does it truly constitute this fundamental principle. The Way does not reside in words and letters, yet the Tripitaka has continued without interruption until the present day, circulating through ten thousand generations.
The Teaching is the textual expression of the principle for realizing the School; one says that the School enters the Teaching. The School is the essential articulation for penetrating the Teaching;
one says that the Teaching clarifies the School. For those of later learning, these essentials must not be dispensed with. However, the faculties of the ancients were sharp.
The saliva has been spilled and leaked; coming and going, it universally guides later worthies. When the power of mental liberation is thick, one stirs oneself with vigilance and practices the path.

When the conditions reach their culmination, there is a sudden, vast, and penetrating realization. This is then transformed into the transmission of the "clothing of superior practice," which extends through successive generations, continuing the source and flow of the ancestral lamp.
To sincerely believe in and uphold [this teaching]—as seen in the Recorded Sayings of Shiwu—is rare in recent times; the former masters have departed.
The times were distant, yet his traces remain as his calligraphy flows on. Reading these characters, one knows that the inner words of the ancients are not to be treated lightly.

This ancient master lived in the mountains for thirty years, his feet never crossing the threshold. He had completely forgotten the mundane world; his pure will was firm and serene. He did not harbor worldly gain in his breast.

When a single fragment of cloud vanished, he returned to the numinous peaks. Expounding even half a verse, his mind was as bright as the moon; he parted the hairs of his pen with a stroke of brilliance.

The Celestial River flows with boundless, deep currents; from it surges forth a single spring of the water of wisdom, flowing out from a treasury of jewels. It courses across the mountain peaks and wanders freely beyond the clouds.

This is truly not a matter of clinging to breath in cold meditation while the withered roots remain unsevered, nor is it like one sitting in a well observing the sky and remaining ignorant of what lies beyond.
This old man is truly a descendant of the Tathāgata’s lineage, a single breath of the Dharma at its end. Thus, by Qing.
The Great Master Jian, looking up to the ancient style of the Way, was filled with joy and inspiration upon hearing of it; his delight in seeking it out was beyond measure.

Having long hoped for its publication and circulation, he later obtained a copy and carved it for distribution. May all who encounter this text experience the awakening of the broad and long tongue [of the Buddha].

May those traveling on the crooked paths of the world find their steps entirely set right. May those with wisdom tread the land of non-action, and may they all, without anxiety, transcend to the higher vehicle.

The urgency of the precepts is such that worldly forms are easy to distinguish, yet a single characteristic is difficult to discern. It is especially made so that one who is ignorant becomes all-knowing—a rare encounter indeed.
I pray that you will joyfully grant me the opportunity to hear this.

The Thirteenth Year of the Guangxu Reign. Re-engraved edition of the *Stone House (Shiwu) Yulu*. Compiled while dwelling in seclusion at the rural village of Yuetaang. Respectfully preface by the disciple-monks studying under him, Zhiyou and others.
Compiled by the Disciples of the Dharma: Stone House Master Guṇabhadra of Fuyuan. Volume One.
Edited by the Disciples of the Path, Zhiyou and others.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the year of Xunwei of the Yuantong era, the Master entered the monastery. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said, "The doors and windows stand wide open;
who is facing the hall? He let out a shout.
Buddha Hall. Because of me, you receive my prostration. One who falls down must rise up by oneself. The magpie cries upon the tree; its intent lies within the hemp field.
Entering the room, he held up his staff and said: "All the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, and all the old monks throughout the world, have all been proclaiming..."
"Seeking duckweed and dust at the bottom of the water; plucking willow blossoms from amidst the fire. As for the New Source of Blessings—how is it?
He planted his staff and gave a shout.
Nian held up the memorial from the Guangjiao Prefecture and said, "The old Gautama has a case that remained unresolved for two thousand years;
today, the Senior Monk Gong shall settle it in the hands of the official of the Guangjiao Prefecture. He presented the memorial, stating: "This submission is made in accordance with the facts."
Holding up the mountain gate, he said in his discourse: "The size of the cauldron and the length of the ladle handle are matters for one's own household; why need they be deliberated upon?
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "Whether it be the precious throne of devas and humans or a curved wooden bed, if I wish to sit upon it now, I shall simply sit. Furthermore...
Without performing a prostration to the King of Mount Sumeru, he ascended the seat. Having finished offering incense and making prayers for the Emperor, he next held up the incense and said:
"This single portion of incense, burned within the burner, is offered to the late Great Monk of the Chan Temple and the Hermitage in Huzhou Road Daochang, to repay the kindness of the Dharma-milk.
He then said: "When held fast, not even a trace of its edge is revealed; when released..."
Walking, the ten directions intersect both vertically and horizontally; meeting in the depths of water and clouds, yet it is atop a thousand peaks.
Meeting atop a thousand peaks, yet it is in the depths of water and clouds. This very day, within Fuyuan Temple, the hall is opened and the Dharma is expounded.
Yesterday, by the side of Tianhu Hermitage, I broke ground and tilled the soil amidst the mist. Thus it is said: "The Dharma has no fixed form;
when meeting conditions, it becomes the source. This may transmit the wind of true stillness and assist, from afar, the transformation of non-action.
At such a time as this, what is it? [He raises his staff and strikes once. A nine-myriad-li peng-bird spreads its wings; a thousand-year-old crane soars aloft.

Again, he raised the matter of the Three Sages’ Way: "When I meet a person, I come forth; when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others. When I propagate the Way of Transformation, I meet a person and do not come forth;
when I come forth, I then act for the sake of others. The Master said: "As for me, the mountain monk, today—am I acting for the sake of others, or am I not acting for the sake of others?
If you say I am acting for the sake of others, then you wrong the Three Sages. If you say I am not acting for the sake of others, then..."
"Even those who are humble and lowly are brought to flourish and transformation. But how can one reach the state of perfect adequacy? [The Master] strikes the whisk and says:
"The Rong, Yi, Man, and Mo peoples are divided among various nations; all are contained within the transformative nourishment of our Sovereign."

That evening, during the informal discourse (xiaochan), [the Master said]: "The assembly gathered here has long resided within the monastic groves, speaking of 'studying Chan' and 'cultivating the Way.
Yet they fail to realize that prior to the arising of a single thought, there is nothing else whatsoever. The moment you attempt to direct the mind, you have already erred."
Master Xuefeng ascended Mount Touzi three times and visited Dongshan nine times; he was like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage, not knowing how much wear and tear he inflicted upon his feet.
If you now wish to attain what is already perfected, look directly within yourself—what else is there?
When there is nothing to do, do not falsely seek; if you gain something through false seeking, it is ultimately not gained at all.

Again, he cites the words of Master Nanyuan: "Since my youth, I have herded a water buffalo. If I intend to herd it on the east bank of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass;
if I intend to herd it on the west bank of the stream, I likewise cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass.
It is better to simply accept things as they are, yet even this leaves nothing to be seen. The verse says: "Nanyuan’s herding has no..."
East and West, on both banks the spring breeze makes the green grass grow level and uniform; all this is the soil and water of the National House.
It is better to simply accept whatever comes as it is.
Upon ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: before the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the nights are short and sleep is insufficient; on the fifteenth day of the fourth month...

After the days grew longer, there was more than enough food. On the very fifteenth day of the fourth month, the Zen monks within Fuyuan Temple had their porridge sufficient, their rice sufficient, and their sleep sufficient;
they played in the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment and dwelt in the samādhi of the Wisdom of Equality.
I dare ask you all: by what cause did they reach such a state? When the fragrant breeze enters the door, it is of itself...
A Coolness Arises. The lake water reaching the gate was not intentional.
[The Master] thanked the special envoy and the head seat of the Three Pagodas Monastery in the capital. He ascended the hall and said:
"Muzhou inciting Linji to eat a blow of the staff was not a kind heart. Yangqi pressing Ciming for the evening sermon was not a kind heart. Zhaozhou visiting the Way..."
I am not being kind-hearted. Fuyuan’s special messenger is forcing me to take up residence in this monastery. Now tell me: is this a kind heart or not?
"Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow; half are for missing you, half are for resenting you."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If we discuss this matter, it is like a farmer tilling a field. If one tills deeply and sows at the proper time, the harvest will surely be abundant.
Beyond what is paid to the government and provided for oneself, there will be ample surplus. This is due to nothing other than diligent effort.
If one does not till deeply and sows at the wrong time, the harvest will surely be meager. Beyond what is paid to the government and provided for oneself..."
Those who are insufficient within themselves have no other cause; it is simply due to being mired in indolence.
Yet, instead of blaming their own indolence for the resulting lack of what they require, they instead envy others for obtaining much through diligent effort. Such people are truly to be pitied.
What is the intent behind the *Fukuen Setsuwaku* (The Discourse on the Source of Fortune)? It is not that one intends to strike the grass, but rather seeks to startle the deer.
Śe, the Hall Master, and the Cleaners, please attend. Entering the hall: When one body is pure, many bodies are pure; when one world is pure, many worlds are pure.
From where does the foul odor of the latrine come? From where does the dust and tumbleweed in the Buddha Hall arise? What is it that...?
[He] arrived at his place. Covering his nose with his hand, he said, "There is yet another point.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "Three months of summer retreat, one month has passed. In these gardens and groves, the green shade is abundant.
The croaking of frogs remains only within the ponds; I ask you, practitioners of Zen, do you understand? This very Dharma-body of our school—its purity lies in hearing."
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva buys sesame cakes with money; upon setting them down, they turn out to be steamed buns. [The Master] strikes the whisk and says:
"To provide flour, one must return to the wheat of his native province; to sing the song, one must be a man from the imperial capital."
Ascending the hall at the ceremony for scattering green seedlings, [the Master said]: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil;

the Sage attains the One and the world is in peace. When a patch-robed monk attains the One, every matter is already perfected. Holding up his staff, he said: "This staff attains the One and moves about freely and spontaneously.
In the evening, taking a stroll upon East Lake, it points with a smile to the rice seedlings, all one color of green."
Again, [the Master] raised the occasion when Yangshan was working in the fields with Guishan. Yangshan said, "This end is so low; that end is so high.
Guishan said, "Water can level things; simply use water to level them. Yangshan said, "Water is not reliable either.
Simply let the high places be level with the high, and the low places be level with the low. Guishan approved of this. The verse says: "Fragmented patches, high and low, are all fields."
What partiality is there in the vision of Master Miu-shan and his son? At Fu-yuan, hands do not even touch mud or water; sitting and watching the harvest, it surpasses that of last year.
Small Precept Lifting Assembly Small Session Sermon: Knowing without touching phenomena, the cricket cries by the golden well-railing; without confronting conditions...
Illumination. Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, autumn has already arrived early. The boundless realms of all lands are unified within a single mote of dust;
there is not a single mote of dust that is not the great ocean of Perfect Enlightenment. The ten ages of past and present are melted into a single thought-moment;

there is not a single thought that is not the season of self-liberation. To proceed in this very way is to not enter the path of travel. How much more so when one carries the staff across the shoulder and wears the robes tightly fastened?
Straw sandals; footprints in every direction, ten thousand miles from home.
This is called wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and hills, seeking teachers and visiting paths to practice Zen—all of this is merely running about in deluded madness.
Even if you were to leap up to the thirty-third heaven in a single instant, traveling across billions of Mount Sumerus and billions of fragrant oceans, take up your staff.
He struck the desk once and said: "One cannot depart from this very place.
At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month. A cool breeze opens my bamboo door;
atop the ridge, patches of white clouds—one here, two there—are blown by the wind until they are scattered in all directions. Lightly drifting and floating, they seem on the verge of dissolving."
It does not disperse; though one wishes to gather it, it will not gather. The old monk beckons toward the white clouds: "White clouds, white clouds, why do you not stay?
In the end, you must return to the mountains from whence you came. Wandering abroad at the ends of the earth along the roads. *He lets out a shout.*
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, Master Xie presided over the assembly and ascended the hall, saying: “The moon in the heavens is perfectly full; the moon among men is but half-full.
If you people do not yet know this, I shall strike the drum and invite everyone to look together. To say it is the *maṇi* jewel within the Tathāgata-garbha is one thing;
yet it is also like the lapis lazuli bowl in the hands of Venerable Piṇḍola. It cannot be compared, nor can it be distinguished. The celestial wind...”
The wind blows upon the dew, moistening the osmanthus blossoms; the fragrance soaks the Hall of Broad Cold at the edge of the clouds.
Entering the hall: Bodhidharma dwelt at Shaolin for nine years facing the wall—his defenses were not secure. Shushan sold his cotton robe.
From a thousand li away one sees people; at the head of the road, it is cluttered and complex. Here at Fuyuan, the walls and moats are firm and secure;
the path is level and straight. All you people, every day you walk upon the correct road and dwell in a place of stability and security.
Yet, why is it that this single plot of land in the middle cannot be trodden?
Again, he raised a case where a monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the pure Dharma-body? The ancient worthy replied, "If one has no minor servants at home, one cannot be considered a gentleman.
The Master said, "All you Zen practitioners, when the ancients answered this way, they were very much like those who mistake a servant for their master.
Today, if someone were to ask Fuyuan, 'What is the pure Dharma-body?', I would simply answer him: [the text here implies a specific response]."
A household has no second master.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, ascending the hall, it would have been quite pleasant staying within the mountains; instead, you have pointlessly entered the noisy marketplace.
Sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline; that single bright star was the source of calamity.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I have a single phrase that I wish to explain thoroughly for all of you. Yet, I fear you might revile me, so I do not explain it for you.
Again, I fear you might doubt me, so let it be as it is now: whether I speak it or do not speak it.
He stroked his knee and said, "Whether you understand me or condemn me, I have no words of apology."

Ascending the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat: For ninety days we shared the same restriction of the feet; today is the day of *pravāraṇā*. In the evening rain, the temple’s green lamps flicker;

in the western wind, the white stone bridge stands. A solitary body clad in the three robes, a single light bundle for ten thousand miles. If you should arrive at the place of Muzhou, you must beware the blade hidden within his smile.
A Small Sermon on the Eve of the New Year: The year has ended, and the month has ended; the thirty-six cycles of time have exhausted all skillful means.

Their total eradication depends entirely upon the five-watch bell. When one is in poverty, there is change; when there is change, there is penetration. It is the same moon before the window as ever, yet as soon as the plum blossoms appear, it is no longer the same.
Under the three wooden rafters, the sons of Chan—both their bags empty and their bowls empty—pick up what is discarded.
Wearing a tattered robe of hempen rags, one is unaware that the body dwells within a state of profound stillness. Only the staff of Fuyuan does not belong to the workings of yin and yang;
it is entirely free from the cycles of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. From antiquity to the present, it supports heaven and sustains earth.
Walking together and sitting together, it whistles at the moon and chants with the wind—who cares for you whether the rivers and lakes roll on or the sun and moon race by? Wait.
Leaning idly against the corner of the meditation seat, a black dragon hangs within a single mass of cloud.
On the first day of the year, he ascends the hall. Jingqing said, "On this New Year’s Day, there is Buddha-dharma. Mingjiao said, "On this New Year’s Day, there is no Buddha-dharma.
To say it exists does not necessarily mean it exists; to say it does not exist does not necessarily mean it does not exist. It is like Zhang Gong drinking wine.
Master Li was intoxicated. Zhaozhou hung a gourd on the eastern wall.
He ascended the hall and said: "The spring wind opens the bamboo door; the night rain drips onto the heart of the flower.

One by one, I have revealed the supreme function for all of you and expounded the primary principle. Why do you not understand? After a long silence, he said: "Do not blame this mountain monk for being too busy. Guang.
The shadows seem like arrows, secretly urging us on.
On the Lantern Festival, Xie Dongban Dianzhu and Wunian Xitang address the assembly from the high seat: "To advance is by means of propriety; to retreat is by means of propriety."
Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me. Rotten ginger and aged soapberry pods;
old colanders and broken wooden ladles. Selling cheap in the east and selling dear in the west—whether there is profit or loss, it never leaves the marketplace.
Last night, the "True Person of No Rank" brandished a vajra-ring and spurred on a flying dragon-horse, galloping across the four continents.
Yet he now shares the Lantern Festival with Master Huánzhōng inside the eye of a gnat. At dawn, as he rises, he is still right here upon this very lump of flesh.
Striking his staff once, he says: "I behold the lamp-light Buddha’s original radiant auspiciousness."
Thus it was.

From the Buddha’s Nirvana until he ascended the hall [to give his final teaching], for seventy-nine years, he dangled empty fabrications. On the fifteenth day of the second month, there was one great, decisive blow.
Even if one could hide one's entire body, one cannot avoid exposing both feet. Before the assembly of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, the clouds disperse and the waters part.

The flow [of the teaching] continues. When the sixteen-foot golden body has vanished like smoke and fire extinguished, Kāśyapa returns to Mount Kukkuṭapāda, and the jealous heart of the Māra king finally rests.
O virtuous ones, do you wish to see the Old Man Śākyamuni? (He strikes the meditation staff once and says:
"Spring breezes fill the earth with peach and plum blossoms; the red are naturally red, and the white are naturally white."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing is the very root of ignorance. To have no seeing within seeing and knowing—this is nirvana.

The spring mountains layer upon layer in chaotic green; the spring waters ripple through the void in azure blue. Vast and empty between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach?
He held up his staff and said, "I let Shakyamuni Buddha pass. He struck the floor with the staff and said, "I pierce Xuedou’s nostrils through. After a long silence, he remained still.
It is said: "The sword leaves its precious sheath because of injustice; the medicine emerges from the golden jar to save the sick.
On the occasion of the Buddha-bath ceremony, the Master ascends the hall and cites the World-Honored One’s first appearance after birth:

with one finger pointing to heaven and one finger pointing to earth, he took seven steps and looked around in the four directions, saying, "In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the Honored One. The verse says: Pointing to heaven...
Pointing to the ground, he says, "It is the sun. He speaks with self-importance as if no one else existed. When one has spirit, one adds even more spirit;
the fragrant mists fill the garden, moistening the loquats.
Small Precept Ceremony (Xiaocan) for the Retreat. Tomorrow morning we enter the retreat; tonight is the small precept ceremony.
I, Fuyuan, am not Langyao, yet I shall point out the five kinds of illnesses. Xiyuan deliberated on two errors. For the ninety days of this summer retreat, you must not take a single step recklessly.
During the twelve hours of each day, you must not give rise to a single thought. Do not give rise to a single thought.

And one immediately realizes non-arising. Without moving a single step, one wanders throughout the sands of all worlds. Practicing in this manner, there is not a single day that is not a state of settled dwelling (*an-guan*).
One can naturally laugh and enjoy oneself amidst the forests and springs; who cares about sitting and letting the years and months pass?
Just as it is, yet not just as it is. Have you not seen Master Yunmen say: "It reaches the point where the entire universe and great earth are without even a hair’s breadth..."
To eliminate even the slightest fault is merely the "turning phrase. Not seeing a single dharma is still but half the task;

one must further know that there is a time for the "complete raising" of the upward path. (He strikes the meditation staff once. "I love the length of summer days; everyone else suffers from the scorching heat."
Ascending the hall for the commencement of the retreat: Before you all entered the retreat, you could go to Tiantai, Nanyue, Emei, or Wutai whenever you wished, and return whenever you wished.
Why is it that after the retreat has commenced, you have no further use for your straw hats, satchels, grass sandals, or staffs?
*Poke!* Do not say that the mouth of the bag is no longer in the hands of this mountain monk!
Ascending the hall: Before the fifteenth day, the nights are short and sleep is insufficient; after the fifteenth day, the days are long and hunger is more than enough.
On the fifteenth day itself, the rice is as white as snow and the fans are as round as the moon. Fanning themselves while eating rice, they still complain that it is hot.
Śākyamuni the Old One said: "For one who knows contentment, even lying upon the ground is peaceful and happy."

Those who lack contentment will find no satisfaction even if they dwell in heaven. It is further said: "Even if one were to pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created will not be forgotten;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself. This is most certain.
If there were no retribution for good and evil, then Heaven and Earth would surely be partial.
Again, the King of East India invited Prajñātāra for a meal. During the meal, he said to the Patriarch, "All the other monks recite sutras;
why is it that you alone do not recite sutras? The Patriarch replied, "When the breath goes out, it does not involve external conditions;
when the breath comes in, it does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates. I constantly recite such a sutra as this—hundreds of thousands of millions of volumes—not merely one or two."
The Master said: "O virtuous practitioners of Zen! When Prajñātāra answered in such a manner, he healed the sores on people's eyes but gouged out the flesh from their hearts.
If someone were to ask Fuyuan, 'All the monks here are reciting sutras; why does the Elder not recite them? I would simply answer him:
'By the window in broad daylight, under the moon in the azure sky—when you wish to recite, you recite; when you wish to stop, you stop.'"
Stop. Now tell me: is there any difference in quality between this and Prajñātāra? If you can discern this, I grant that you possess the "one eye."
On the anniversary of Master An’s death, I offer incense. It has its origins, yet it lacks any handle. It was picked up from atop a meditation cushion at West Peak Temple in Jianyang Mountain.
It has no eyes and no ears; it has no head and no tail. If you call it a single lump of dough, that is not quite right.
When one smells it, there is no fragrance. One must not broadcast the family’s shame to the outside world; a man of clarity does not perform deeds in secret.
Entering the hall: Huangmei had Old Lu tread the rice-mortar; Shitou criticized Yaoshan for not doing so. There is a ten-foot-tall thistle.
One may command the winds from all eight directions, yet without a three-foot whip, it is difficult to control a horse of a thousand *li*.
In a garden of *eranda* (Ilan), sandalwood does not grow; atop a *āmalaka* (Huangbo) tree, how could there be honeyed fruit?
Ascending the hall, he said: "Movement is like drifting clouds; stillness is like the spirit of the valley. The salty taste within water; the blue lacquer within color.
Fine rain wets one’s clothes, yet it cannot be seen; flowers fall upon the ground, yet there is no sound to hear."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Divine radiance is never obscured; its sublime legacy endures for ten thousand ages. Seek it only within yourself; do not look for it outwardly.
The intent of raising a rooster lies in the fifth watch of the night."
Ascending the hall, he said: "That which is heard cannot be heard; that which is seen cannot be seen. Last night at the fifth watch, the wind blew down a petal of peach blossom.
Crimson clouds arise upon the surface of the gray moss; though the hundred birds do not come, spring is in full bloom."
Ascending the hall, he said: "I am originally but a clumsy bhikṣu of the mountain forests; I have come here at leisure to join the company of fellow meditators.

Even if we gather together and our human relations are harmonious, what human affection can last to the very end? Enough, enough, enough! Green mists and red clouds form a brocade of a thousand peaks."
The west wind and yellow leaves: autumn fills the heavens. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The moon emerges from the eastern sea-gate; its golden ripples stretch vast and wide. Perfect and perfect, it suffers no loss; bright and bright, it shines with excellence.
I send word to the old White Hare: tell this to Lady Cháng'ér. Gather your radiance, do not delay; you must conceal your light."
Act early; do not wait until black clouds gather from all four directions and the radiance of the heavens has vanished entirely.
In this world, there is only the mind of the Way-man, which remains ever-luminous from kalpa to kalpa until now.
Master Xie, the Librarian, ascends the hall: "Today is the fifteenth day of the eighth month; The trees wither and leaves fall in the golden wind.
The den of the wild fox is the palace of the Brahma King; The dog’s tail writes the *svastika* character. From where do the Great Canon and the Small Canon come?"
Holding up his staff, he said: "All flow forth from this very place. To casually utter a single *bhrāṅ* cuts off the idle proclamations of past and present.
He ascended the hall and said: "Day after day, again day after day; two, three, four, five, eight, nine, ten. Counting until the red [leaves] have fallen."
In the deep green of spring, once again it is the first day of the fourth month. Morning drags on, evening drags on;

before one's eyes lies the ocean-treasury of Vairocana, yet one abandons it to grasp at a single floating bubble. Enough, enough! If the cultivation of the mind does not reach the ground of no-mind, then myriad things and a thousand variations will merely drift away with the current.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To eat, one must satisfy hunger; to drink, one must quench thirst; to wear clothes, one must ward off the cold;
to return home, one must reach the destination. To study the Way, one must reach the place where the Buddhas of the three periods cannot open their mouths;
to practice Zen, one must reach the place where the patriarchs of the world cannot set foot. If you do not do so, you are merely leaning upon others' gateways and huddling against others' walls."

To listen to others' commands and swallow their spit—this is not the mark of a true man. When Fuyuan speaks thus, he shows that good medicine is bitter to the taste and loyal words are harsh to the ear.
When the Head Seat Kōgan-in arrived, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Muzhou incited Linji to ask Huangbo about the Great Meaning of the Buddha-dharma;
three times he received sixty blows of the staff. The mouth is indeed a gateway to calamity. Is there anyone here who can avoid this fault?"
After a long while, he said: "The empty one sits beneath the cliff; from heaven, the four flowers fall. Ascending the hall, he said:
"In the sixth and seventh months, the heavens do not rain. The farmers are busy day and night pumping water. Their backs are cracked and parched, their feet ache;
their eyes grow dim and they are too weak, on the verge of fainting from exhaustion. Then the officials come to press for the summer tax. The silk for the tax must be paid."
They calculate their travel expenses; they demand repayment of barley and wheat to their heart’s content. They fail to provide for the three daily meals. Consider us who have left the household life:
we do not recognize the provisions already at hand. There is not a single point of dedication in our bodies or minds toward the Path.
We wander aimlessly to the east and frolic to the west. Three or five of us sit together in a huddle; as soon as we open our mouths, we speak of the faults of others.
Once one has returned to the dark chamber of the body, there is no unrighteousness or shameful act that will not be committed.

Do not say you have merely fallen among the lower realms; in your next life, you will surely become a farmer tilling the soil. The suffering previously described is such that it cannot be compared to the present time.

An ancient worthy had a single word for instructing his disciples; I bring it forth now before this assembly of humans and devas: "Not a single inch of the field of the monastic robes [has been cultivated]."
The merit of a single basket of earth. Iron Mountains collapse; the bitterness of a hundred punishments. Entering the hall:
"If no one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, even with wisdom one cannot comprehend it. To open one's mouth is already not it.
"In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. Not opening one's mouth is also not it. Five horses do not neigh; a single ox [does not bellow].
Drinking water. Whether opening the mouth or not opening the mouth, it is neither right nor wrong. "The benevolent see it and call it benevolence;
the wise see it and call it wisdom. Entering the hall:
Baizhang taught people to cultivate fields, leaving his entire body covered in mud and water. Foyan directed the monks to perform construction, leaving the ground covered [in dust].
Muzha. Yangqi pressed Ciming during the evening session, saying: "One who has achieved the Way is not at ease. Zhaozhou taught Yanxiang to let go, saying:
"One who is at ease does not achieve the Way. Fuyuan speaks thus: this too is merely increasing delusion for the sake of others' idle affairs.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Whether saint or ordinary person, as soon as you enter the gate, you see the nostrils of the Persian;
as soon as you open your eyes, you see the heart and liver of the clam; as soon as you open your mouth, you see everyone’s two eyebrows resting horizontally across their faces.
Why then do you fail to see them? For those with clear eyes, there is darkness three feet before them."

Rising from illness, he ascended the hall and said: "I cite the Ancestor of Tea Creek (Zhaozhou), who addressed the assembly, saying: 'I have a great illness, which is not cured by worldly physicians.
Later, a monk asked Caoshan, 'I wonder, what kind of illness is this? Caoshan replied, 'It is the illness that cannot be gathered together.'"
He asked again, "Do all sentient beings also have this illness? Caoshan said, "I, this old monk, am currently searching for its point of origin and cannot find it.
The Master said, "This monk is one who has experienced the illness himself; he searches with great intensity, not letting go even when reaching the tip of a hair.
Were it not for Caoshan, who knows where it falls, others would find it difficult to open their mouths. Furthermore...
He composed a verse and presented it to the assembly: "A hundred bones ache and throb, crowded together in pain; One bout of heat follows one bout of cold.
Though I seek its point of origin, I find it not at all; The medicinal cauldron and the wind-fueled stove have both been overturned."
Winter Solstice Small Sermon. Dongshan removed the fruit table; his sense of acceptance and rejection was not yet forgotten.
Yuquan did not wash his cotton trousers; his stubborn adherence was difficult to sever. At a place like Fuyuan Temple, this is the very season:

therein it is different from the plum blossoms’ solitary elegance, yet the dark fragrance continues to drift. As the thread adds to the cold shadows, we encounter once more this auspicious scene to welcome spring. Within the lanterns...
A hat. Blowing a sheng flute from the bottom of the water. A dew-pillar putting on a robe. Dancing amidst the clouds. Do you all understand this?
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month is Qingming; Qingming comes after the Cold Food Festival.
Again, he cites a monk’s question to an ancient worthy: "What is the meaning of winter’s arrival? The Worthy replied, "The capital produces great yellow [rhubarb]. The verse says:

When asked about the meaning of winter’s arrival, The capital produces great yellow. In the earthen stove, the fire burns deep into the night; The tea is finished, and the fragrance permeates the jar.
Xie Dusi ascended the hall for the winter retreat, together with the *vinaya-dhara*. Each one pervades all, and all pervade each one.
In the world of Gandhavatī, the Buddha’s work is performed through fragrant food; here in Jambudvīpa, the Buddha’s work is performed through sound.

In the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the mallet strikes; in the western continent of Aparagoyānī, all are summoned. In Huai Prefecture, the ox eats the grain; in Yi Prefecture, the horse’s belly swells.
Coarse food satisfies easily; chewing finely makes hunger hard to quell. I only fear it is not jade; if it is jade, how truly marvelous!
On the anniversary of Master An’s passing, he offered incense and said: "At the place where we meet in ill fortune, West Peak and Jianyang—how many matters of unease there are!
They are all contained within this single burner of incense."
On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall. In the bell tower, hymns were chanted; beneath the bed-frame, vegetables were planted.

The Head Seat Sheng said, "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road. At Fuyuan, here, songs are sung to celebrate the New Year at the mountain gate, while sutras are recited to offer blessings to the Emperor within the Buddha Hall.
All these are but sounds, yet they hold infinite meanings—some are worth listening to, others are not. Have you all ever examined this?
"Can you discern it? [The Master] lets out a shout and descends from his seat.
On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascends the hall: "In Jambudvīpa, sound is used as a Buddha-work. When drums are struck in ten directions, they are heard simultaneously in all ten places.
When I ascend the hall at Fuyuan Temple, every single thing is heard at Xilin Temple. Xilin...
Reciting the Buddha’s name within a temple—every single instance can be heard at Fuyuan Temple. Whether one offers praise, one gains a portion of merit;
whether one slanders, one also gains a portion of merit. One is all, and all is one.
At the Lantern Festival in Yinghu Market, why is it that while the eastern neighbor lights his lanterns, the western neighbor sits in the dark? You cannot understand this either, nor can I.
One cannot fathom this principle. It is like soaking a winter melon in cold water; everyone is muddying the waters together. When the Buddha ascended the hall after his *parinirvāṇa*, he said:
"When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world; when body, speech, and mind are impure, [this is not]."
This is called the Buddha’s nirvāṇa. Human sentiments cannot be perfectly harmonized; the world rarely achieves full union.
Days grow long and nights grow short; autumn is hot and winter is cold. A single tangle of willow filaments cannot be gathered up; it remains draped with mist upon the jade balustrade.
Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Sage’s birthday: "The peach of immortality blooms once every three thousand years; the Sage appears once every five hundred years.
Holding up his staff, he said, "The peach of immortality has bloomed! He struck the ground with the staff and said, "The Sage has appeared! He leaned the staff against the wall and remained silent.
All under heaven is at peace.
For the commencement of the retreat, I ascend the hall. At the Fuyuan Monastery, today we begin the retreat; I cannot but establish a regulation for all of you. First:
from morning until evening, whether lifting or setting your feet, you must not tread upon the grounds of the monastery property. Should you tread upon the monastery grounds...
"First: one will certainly incur a *pārājika* offense. Second: during the twelve periods of the day, one must not breathe through the nostrils;
if one breathes through the nostrils, one will certainly incur a *pārājika* offense. Third: let us not speak of this matter for now, let us not speak of it.
It will not be too late to leave it until the fifteenth day of the seventh month. How could there ever have been [anything] inside the jar?"
The turtle has run away. Entering the hall, he said:
"Day after day the sun rises in the east; day after day the sun sets in the west. How many times have you witnessed this rising and setting?

And yet, it is already the first day of the fifth month! Alas, you outsider at the gate! I take your hand and try to lead you in, but you will not enter. I drag my staff and return alone; the gate stands open and empty."
Sighing, he addressed the assembly:
"The ancient masters said, 'The first half-month of the summer retreat has ended; what of the water buffalo?
Some say, 'The first half-month of the summer retreat has ended; what of Hanshan? Fuyuan says, 'The first half-month of the summer retreat has ended...'"
The days and months have passed. As for the matter of one’s own self, how is it? Is it perhaps rising early in the morning to wash your face;

having washed your face, eating porridge; having eaten porridge, eating rice; having eaten rice, dismissing the assembly; and having dismissed the assembly, falling asleep? Is that the matter of one’s own self?
Is it perhaps being on the eastern corridor, the western corridor, inside the quarters, or at the head of the mountain gate? Or is it the sounding of the drum?
Is fanning the flames of right and wrong your own personal affair?
Is it perhaps reading the various schools of thought, examining long and short compositions, engaging in lofty talk and grand discourse as if no one else were present—this your own personal affair?

Is it perhaps calculating within the sutras, speculating upon the recorded sayings, claiming to have attained what you have not attained, or claiming to have realized what you have not realized—this your own personal affair?
Is it not a matter of performing several prostrations before the Buddha, reading several scrolls of scripture, burning two fingers, or lighting several sticks of incense on the crown of the head?
Is this deceiving the world and seeking profit and offerings—this what is truly within one's own person? Is it not simply a matter of sitting upon the long benches of the monastic hall?
With eyes closed and brows knit, drifting in a state of profound dullness and bewildered confusion, you let the seasons pass by in vain. Is this truly your own fundamental matter?
In such a state, you are not even equal to a man from a village of three households who drags his plow;

he tills the fields and sows the land to provide for his livelihood and sustain his body, yet he incurs no fault. We, the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya, rely on the compassionate shade of the Tathāgata, yet we do not plow.

They eat their food; they wear clothes without raising silkworms. They dwell in high halls and great mansions, with spacious palaces and long corridors. Their ten fingers do not touch water; a hundred affairs do not trouble their minds.
Everything is spontaneously present; every detail is ready at hand. It is simply because it is already present; it is simply because it is ready at hand.
Instead, they indulge in license and negligence, greedily seeking what is unlawful, failing to cultivate the monastic vocation, and remaining impure in their precepts.

Ignorant of cause and effect and fearing neither sin nor merit, they run deep debts within themselves, creating the causes for the hells. When the Old Man of Yama appears, he is devoid of human sentiment and has no face to show;
whether it be a single good or a single evil deed, the master records are crystal clear. Once he arrives, he will settle the accounts with you—down to the very last shred of a turnip.

A single grain of rice, a drop of water, a thread of silk—each must be repaid. For the Source of Blessings to issue such a proclamation is itself to increase ignorance through involvement in trivial matters for others' sake.
Ascending the hall: A single speck of dust arises and the great earth is gathered up. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the mouth of the sack is tied shut.
A single leaf falls and the world beneath is autumn. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the mouth of the sack is untied. At this very moment of *pravāraṇā*, what is there to realize?
What is there to cultivate? Under the soles of the straw sandals is Northern Uttarakuru; at the tip of the staff is Southern Jambudvīpa. Day after day, evening after evening...
Vast and distant; without restraint and without bondage, free and at ease. Suddenly, the old Fenggan appeared and said, "I shall go with you to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
[The other] asked, "And what of that? Shaking his hand, he said, "You are not of my kind."

Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: The dark moon is difficult to see; the bright moon is easy to see. Before black and white are yet distinguished, how is it when the eyes see compared to when the mind sees?
Therefore it is said: "At the moment of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [true] seeing. Seeing is already apart from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. He plants his staff and says:
"Last night the cassia trees in the lunar palace blossomed; a fine breeze blew down their celestial fragrance."
Come. King Zhao’s bleached bones lie buried in green grass; no one sweeps his Golden Terrace. Entering the hall:

To clarify a single thought of empty luminosity is still not to have shed the fetters of the Three Vehicles. To recognize the manifestation in eight places is precisely to be deluded regarding one's own numinous light.
Even if you were to turn your body upon the level ground and shift your steps within a thicket of thorns, your heels—
I would give him thirty blows. Why? If it were not for the woodcutter’s path, how could one reach Ge Hong’s dwelling?

On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, he ascended the hall: The Dipper and the Winged Star shine eternally; heaven and earth are forever tranquil. The wind does not rustle the branches; the rain does not break the clods of earth.
The ruler is a sovereign like Yao and Shun; the customs are those of Cheng and Kang. The Queen Mother of the West unfurls her cloud-banner day and night.
[The Master] turns [the seat]. "In the fourth month on the mountain by the sea, the peaches of immortality ripen.
He ascends the hall and says: "On the first day of the tenth month, the furnace is opened. Everywhere else people speak of cold and heat; at Fuyuan, there is only the ordinary.
We do not know how to arrange or contrive anything. We bury two lumps of charcoal deep down and pile a full furnace of yellow earth."
"Leaves! Do not begrudge that there are few embers; you only need for the warmth to connect. Lower the heavy curtains and seal the cracks in the windows.
Who then cares about the thick frost upon the roof or the deep snow before the courtyard?

As long as there is a single mass of harmonious energy within your own house, you need not listen to the cold words and idle talk outside; let them exhaust themselves on their own. O Zen practitioners, this is the fundamental..."
The mountain-dweller of Shèzhù has not yet left a trace of axe or hatchet upon it.

He ascends the hall and says: "When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. When there is no fault, there are no dharmas; when there is no arising, there is no mind. Therefore it is said:
When this mountain monk dwelt in the hermitage, I saw only the realm of dwelling in the hermitage. The gate faced a thousand peaks, and my mind was at ease."
As for the environment: in the morning one gazes upon drifting white clouds; in the evening one listens to the murmuring of flowing water.
One boils wild herbs in a tripod with broken legs and mends tattered robes beneath a peaked-roof hut.

Free and easy, unbound and unrestrained, the shadows of śāla trees fall upon the celestial lake, and the fragrance of grapevines wafts over the stone terrace. Neither right nor wrong reaches here; fame and profit are utterly forgotten. Thus one dwells.
When I was serving as the head of the monastery, I saw the conditions of that time: the gates connected to the lakeside market, and the grounds bordered by Haizhou.
Rising late and sleeping late, I welcomed guests and saw them off. I established the monastic regulations amidst a state of peril and gathered monks within a place of solitude.
The songs of fishermen and the pipes of cowherds were heard constantly; the mountain colors and stream reflections were rarely seen. The red dust rolled on, and the bright days passed in haste.
Hurry! Tell me: dwelling at a lake temple and residing in a mountain hermitage—are they the same or different? After a long silence, he said: "No mountain goes without its clouds;
every stream contains the moon."
Ascending the hall to pray for rain: I recall last year in the fifth month, when fire-clouds scorched the fields and heaven sent no rain;

every household planted their seeds, hoping for a good harvest this year. Yet I did not expect this year to be like that as well. How magnificent is the heart of these lords, dukes, generals, and ministers!

Their anxiety for the people is as urgent as if it were their own. When they invoked the dragon deities, the spirits were moved by their sincerity, and here in Jambudvīpa, sweet rain has been poured down.
The rain poured down incessantly for three days of continuous deluge. All gods, humans, and living beings were filled with joy. I dare ask you all:
tell me, by whose power and grace was this brought about? [He strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and says: *Suru suru, siri siri.*
Again, it is recounted that a monk asked Qianfeng: "The Buddhas of the ten directions all share the single path to the gate of Nirvana;
I wonder, where does the beginning of this path lie? Qianfeng struck the ground with his staff once and said, "It is right here. The monk reported this to Yunmen.
Yunmen picked up a fan and said, "This fan leaps and bounds up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra, the Lord of the East."
A sea carp is struck with a blow; the rain pours down like an overturned basin. The verse says: The Dragon Gate of ten thousand fathoms opens with a single squeeze;
An overturned basin of sudden rain, aided by wind and thunder. Returning home with the *kāṣāya* soaked through, one looks upon it: Half is red clouds, half is ocean moss.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The venom of a centipede’s feathers is not the true poison; when calculated, it does not equal the poison of the human heart. The heat of the three summer months is not the true heat;
upon reflection, nothing surpasses the heat of the human heart. The Asura King constantly delights in reviling the devas; so too did the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra."
You insist on slandering the Buddha; when the Way rises one chi, the demon rises ten zhang. Your wiles are finite, while my non-acceptance is infinite.
On the first day of the seventh month, he ascended the hall: "Ten days into autumn in the human world, the lake temple already feels cool; the color of the bamboo by the stream is green."
The fragrance of lotuses within a mirror—this very mind is still not it. To treat it as an object and vainly attempt to grasp its measure is futile;
this matter from before the empty kalpa is proclaimed today.

Ascending the hall upon the conclusion of the retreat: Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell; the moonlight on the pavilions vanishes as the clouds disperse. Where there is no Buddha, pass by with haste;
the lotus leaves in the pond are blown apart by the wind. Three thousand miles away, when meeting a person, do not speak of this mistakenly.

The mountains of Langzhou and the waters of Liuzhou; the four seas and five lakes are all within the Imperial Transformation. Thousands upon thousands, waist-bags and straw hats, are asked about them and all speak only of mountains and waters.
Suddenly, one who cannot bear it comes forth and says: "If you speak of mountains, just speak of mountains; if you speak of waters, just speak of waters.
What fault is there in that? After a long silence, he said: "One must not yet cast away this whole heart; when meeting people, for now..."
I shall speak in three parts.
Entering the hall: A man of high standing who has traveled on pilgrimage speaks of "investigating Zen" (chan) and speaks of "cultivating the Way.
This is just like sitting inside a granary and crying out that one is hungry; you are entirely surrounded by food, yet you yourself refuse to eat it—how does this concern anyone else?
What matter is there? Throughout the twelve periods of the day, every movement and every action is entirely one vast highway, free from any thorns or debris to obstruct your heels.
It is simply that you yourself refuse to take a step forward; what does this have to do with others?
What is superior about the Buddhas compared to ordinary people, and what is inferior about ordinary people?
"All Buddhas—since they are great men, so am I. How can you disparage yourself and yield in defeat? [The Master] suddenly picked up his staff and said:
"The Tathāgata has said that what is called a 'unified mass' is not actually a unified mass. Where shall one seek the bright moon and the reeds?
I suspect he is right there upon the autumn river."

Ascending the hall on the Mid-Autumn Festival: The first moon and the fifteenth moon—when it is waning, there is no fullness; when it is full, there is no waning. Fullness and waning do not interfere with one another;
the clear light is ever pure and bright. Last night, the rain and dew were heavy in the Moon Palace; the celestial wind blew down golden flakes.
Again, he cites the Venerable Yan-yang’s question to Zhaozhou: "When not a single thing can be brought forth, what then? Zhaozhou said, "Put it down.
Yan-yang said, "Since not a single thing can be brought forth, what is there to put down? Zhaozhou said, "If you cannot put it down, carry it away. The verse says:
The fragrance drifts from the cassia trees under a full moon; Raindrops fall upon the lotus flowers in mid-autumn. Outside the gate...
Let the seasons change as they will; remain steady and cover your head with your own patchwork robe.

[Ascending the hall: When studying the Way and practicing Zen, if the ground of your mind is not yet clear, your own eye is not yet open, the dust of emotion is not yet shed, and the life-root is not yet severed—what is this like?
It is just like a person with eyes entering a thousand-year-old dark room.
It is similar: although all manner of objects and forms are present before one’s eyes, one ultimately does not know whether they are blue or yellow, red or white, long or short, square or round;
one is dazed and ignorant, in a state of pitch-black darkness.
If it is so, then while wearing the *kāṣāya*, how can one consume the offerings of devas and humans?
Having studied the Way and practiced *chan*, the mind-ground is already clear, the eye of wisdom is already opened, the dust of emotion is already shed, and the life-root is already severed.
What is this exactly like? It is just like a mass of the red sun rolling out from the bottom of the great ocean; a thousand-year dark chamber is illuminated in a single instant.
Illuminating and penetrating all the various objects before one’s eyes—blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round—one understands each clearly and perceives each distinctly.
At that time, it is precisely right to nurture the holy embryo beneath the two rafters and before the seven-foot mat, passing the days in leisure.
Only by acting thus can one truly live as one who wears the *kāṣāya*.

Others receive offerings from devas and humans; yet, even so, one must further understand that beneath the gateway of the source of merit lies a threshold of solid iron—high with no way above it, and vast beyond measure. Those outside who wish to enter cannot gain entry.
As for those within, they are unable to exit even if they wish to do so; one must truly exert some brilliance and apply some effort to leap clear before it can be achieved.
If you hesitate or deliberate, you will either strike your head and bump your brow against things, or fall into pits and ravines.
Do not say it was not said.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall: "The Snowy Mountains are high and deep; enduring the cold, he swallowed hemp and wheat. Having passed six years in this manner, he was truly happy.
Without cause, seeing the morning star, he stubbornly claimed to have attained perfect enlightenment. He shook his sleeves and descended the mountain—how early!"

This is already one step too low. To further speak of "saving sentient beings" is to repeatedly expose one's shackles and ropes. Look at the worldly glory of the world—how can it compare to the joy found in the mountains?
A mistake, a mistake! Every year there is the eighth day of the twelfth month.

Entering the new Sangha Hall for the formal discourse: the straight becomes pillars, the curved becomes beams; within the square, there is the circle, and within the circle, the square—this is the excellence with which the master craftsman selects the materials.
Returning to the circle and dissolving the square, discarding the short and taking the long—this is the subtlety with which the founder establishes the Dharma.
Thus, at Fuyuan Monastery, the pillars and stones were erected in the first month of spring in the year of Bingzi, and the construction was completed.
On the Double Ninth of the Wuyin year, axes and hatchets were applied [to the roof]. The six windows shine brightly, revealing the void-clarity of a single color;
the myriad tiles are scaled together, severing the three kinds of leakage. Looking down, one does not see the ground—this belongs to the "board-carrying" Chan practitioner.
Looking up, one does not see the sky—this permits the hooded patch-robed monk of Old Zhuxi. This is not merely the vow and practice of a single lifetime; it is *jiao* (pride).
Kaśyapa’s majestic radiance suddenly increased ten-thousandfold. Following the Baizhang Conglin regulations, the magnificent permanent monasteries have endured for a thousand years.
Truly, the Buddhas of the ten directions, with one voice and in unison, proclaim these verses: "The Buddha-son dwells in this stage; This is the Buddha’s own enjoyment.
He constantly remains within it, Walking, practicing, sitting, and reclining. Furthermore, Layman Pang spoke:
A verse was offered in praise, saying: "The ten directions gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action (wuwei). This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. Although this is so, Zhang Wujin could not restrain his impatience and came forward, saying:
"All of you understand how to eat fruit from the top of a tree, yet you do not know that the tree is bent over. This is truly not the case.
"I understand. Those who built this hall may have caused harm or benefit; those who dwell in this hall may find profit or suffering.
Such words cannot be blamed on him. Why? Because "if a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely have immediate anxieties.
Let us set this matter aside for a moment. But as for the phrase that brings power to a monk from his own side—how would you say it? Liang.

Jiuyun said: "When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink—there is nothing else to do. Listening to the rain and hearing the wind, I idly strike my mat and sleep. On the occasion of opening the furnace for the assembly, Master Fachang said:
"Today, at Fachang, we open the furnace. Not a single traveling monk is here;

Shan paid his respects and said, "In this life, I have traveled on foot to study Chan; if my realization does not surpass that of Xuedou, I vow never to return home.

One day, Zhi addressed the assembly, saying: "Everyone gathers here to eat a stalk of vegetable soup; call it 'one stalk.'"

he immediately perceived the practical application of Zhizhi’s teaching. He hurried to the abbot’s quarters. Upon seeing him approach, Zhizhi smiled and said, "Congratulations! The Great Matter is now complete.
Yue was so overcome with joy that he could utter not a single word; he simply performed a prostration and withdrew. This is what it means to exhaust oneself for the sake of the assembly.
Exert effort; do not waste even a moment. This is the seventh model for practicing Chan and studying the Way. There is yet an eighth model:

all Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter its perfect clarity; and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon it in this way.

Small Assembly Sermon for the Opening of Retreat: "The ancestral style of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is about to fall to the ground; speaking of it now makes one's heart and gall burst.

Its upholding depends entirely upon us, the descendants, yet we did not expect our descendants to first engage in deception. They wander hither and thither, north and south, in confusion. 昧 (mèi) — Obscured/Deceived.

Yet for this very reason, they busy themselves with miscellaneous affairs; wind and dust fill their eyes, and grime covers their faces. Their karmic consciousness is vast and empty, lacking any foundation.
Even if they happen to lodge in the Sangha hall, they wait until the board sounds before returning to their bedding. In their quarters, they gather together to drum up disputes;
folding their legs upon their cushions, they fall straight into sleep. Deluded clouds hang thick as the sky of their nature darkens; the heart is scorched by the friction of sparks.
Like a boiling cauldron, for a time one remains in a state of silent stagnation and light ease; yet, persisting in darkness, one falls into a state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*).

One refuses to follow the *Baizhang Qinggui*, while diligently lecturing and debating on the scriptures of non-Buddhists. Though cause and effect are distinct, one treats them with indifference; though the retribution of sin and merit is manifest, one feels no fear at all.
Whether moving from one mat to another or shifting from one room to another, such negligence arises entirely from body, speech, and mind. Upon one’s head—
The tiles beneath my feet, the robes upon my body, and the food in my mouth—all have come from the offerings of faithful donors.
If I have not yet accomplished the work of the Path, how shall I consume these gifts? Scratching my own heart, how many truly know shame?
Today the third, tomorrow the fourth; in leisure, my time is utterly wasted. One day old age and sickness will come seeking me, and the Lord of Yama will summon me to death.
When the talisman arrives, the karma created in former lives is not forgotten; from this point on, one falls into the three miserable realms and the seven destinies.
Once the *kāṣāya* robe is lost, it is difficult to obtain again; whereas for those with scales, shells, or feathers, it is easy to don them. Behold the practitioners of the Way in antiquity:

they directly forgot the human world and held fame and profit in light esteem. They boiled yellow *jiǎng* and roasted purple taro; with a single lump of rice and a vessel of water, they sustained their withered bodies.

Merely connecting with the vital breath—though the rocks crumble and the pines wither, one remains ultimately unaware. To cleanse the mind is to make provisions for successive lives; beyond all things, pure leisure is the singular height of excellence.
What need is there for the gold of this world to be considered precious? When the fields of kalpas are emptied, the Buddha-flowers bloom; the fragrant breeze strikes and pierces the mother-born nose.
Having attained the rank of passing the imperial examination within the field where Buddhas are chosen, one plays freely within the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment. This...

Regarding these mountain-dwelling poems, I have had much leisure time in the mountains; in the intervals between my drowsiness, I have occasionally composed gāthās for my own amusement. However, paper and ink were scarce, so they were few.
I did not wish to record this. Yet, the Chan practitioner Yunna requested that I write it down, desiring to know my inclinations within the mountains.

Thereupon, reflecting in stillness, I let my brush flow according to the moment until, without realizing it, the volume was filled. Thus, I closed it and returned it to him. Furthermore, I entrust you with this:
do not use this as an aid for song or verse; rather, you must contemplate its meaning, for therein lies a profound inspiration.
My family lives west of the Xi River; the waters fill the Tianhu Lake and the moon fills the stream. Those who have not yet arrived are all startled by the steepness of the mountains;
only those who have come here know the heights and depths of the paths. Snail-slime clings to the plain walls with its dried shells;
tiger tracks leave fresh prints in the rain-soaked mud. I idly close my thatched gate as the spring days are long; the green paulownia flowers bloom and the partridges cry out.
Though the rustic gate is set, it is never closed; I idly watch the secluded birds as they come and go. A foot of jade is easy to find, yet a thousand-fathom stone is hard to obtain;
gold cannot buy a lifetime of leisure. As the snow melts from the morning peaks, one hears the cold waterfall; when the leaves fall in the autumn forest, the distant mountains appear.
The ancient cypress stands as the mist vanishes and the clear day lasts long; right and wrong do not reach the realm of white clouds.
Weedy graves lie in clusters, submerged by wild mugwort; the ancients who were not yet buried all had gold at their waists. It is better to have no desires than to seek them;

how much higher is the step taken backward than the one pressed forward! The golden-scaled fish, greedy for bait, ends up in the cauldron; the spiritual wing, once out of the cage, soars to the heavens.
The mountain elder pays no heed to the affairs of the red dust; he plants his own green hemp to weave a cloth robe.

Paper windows, bamboo huts, and fences of hibiscus; when guests arrive, mugwort broth serves as tea. One often sees those of pure poverty who are ever joyful, while one rarely hears of those with turbid wealth who are not arrogant and extravagant.

Moving the desk to gaze at the bright moon while reading the sutras, offering to the Buddha with a hairpin and a vase of wildflowers—everyone says the Tushita Heaven above is wonderful, but how could it compare to the home of this old monk?
The Way is propagated by those who embody it; upon whom else can one rely? One’s speech must correspond with one’s conduct. A greedy mind is like the sea—when will it ever be satisfied?
Delusive thoughts are like sprouts, increasing day by day. How many plum trees have there been for the pure hermit? How many gardens of taro have there been for the joyful cloister-monk?
Nowadays, those who dwell in mountain huts merely following custom see the Way but forget the mountains, as if they had never known them at all.

To move is to deviate from the truth; to remain still is to err. This realm beyond conceptual thought is even more perplexing. A mind devoid of intention does not yet accord with the Patriarch’s intent;
any state of discursive thought is entirely the demon of affliction. In a low-roofed cottage, the morning sun brings little cold; in a sparse fence, the chrysanthemums yield much late fragrance.
The white clouds drift slowly like trailing silk ribbons, only to be blown across the green creepers by the wind.
Beneath the pines, the double doors stand cold and unfastened; within a single shrine, a golden image is lit by a green lamp.

Wild deer sleeping among the clouds startle from their dreams; monkeys falling into the mountain stream break the vines. When one finds joy in gazing at the mountains, the mountains grow ever more beautiful; when one is free of mind, one merges with the Way, and they accord in harmony.
Having not gone toward the gate for a long time, layers upon layers of moss and lichen have accumulated.
For over thirty years I have dwelt in Yanxi; the work of the mattock has never deceived me. In one garden, the spring colors ripen tea and bamboo shoots;
by several trees, the autumn winds age chestnuts and pears. At night, when the moon is bright atop the mountain, I let out long cries;
when the clouds are warm by the water, I walk alone. My old friends mostly dwell within the fields of fame; with my bamboo door always open, for whom do I wait?
Emerald caverns and vermilion cliffs line all four sides; a thatched hut sits precisely in the center. A single body in coarse cotton robes is warm;
a hundred thoughts have dissolved, and time is forgotten. The rocks are lean, yet the *pǔ* leaves planted there are fine; the soil is deep, and the bamboo sprouts bursting forth grow long.
Sometimes at midnight one hears the sound of bells and chimes, knowing there is a monastery below.
Do not say that dwelling in the mountains brings freedom; there is not a single day when one does not harbor sorrow. By the bamboo, the old woman constantly steals the shoots;
in the wheat fields, the children intentionally let the cattle loose. Grasshoppers and earthworms damage the vegetable sprouts; wild boars and mountain mice devour the grain heads.
When one's actions do not go as intended, one can only accept it and let it rest within oneself.

The hermitage dwells at the very summit of the Misty Peak; its crags and precipices are so perilous that few people travel there. Carrying firewood to the market, the green moss is slippery beneath one’s feet;
bearing rice up the mountain, white sweat flows down one’s back. Since the needs of mouth and body can never be fully satisfied, one should practice frugality;
as time is limited, do not indulge in greed. This old monk does not speak these words out of idle anxiety; I simply wish for all of you to let go and rest.

Twenty years of whistling at the moon and sleeping among the clouds; I pity myself for my old age as I witness the hardships of these times. When crows come seeking food, they stand upon the living altar;
when monks go out to beg for alms, they return with empty bowls. People scramble to scoop up shrimp and clams from the white waters; I, meanwhile, use my hoe to dig into the green mountains.
The yellow rhizomes are exhausted, but the pine blossoms remain; no idle sorrows dwell within my heart.
Living in seclusion, I have naturally parted ways with the world. Moss grows thick and the forest is deep, where the fragrance of plants and trees pervades.

The mountain colors can always be seen through rain and sunshine, yet the clamor of the marketplace is rarely heard from dawn until dusk. I brew tea at a clay hearth by burning yellow leaves; I mend my robes on a rocky terrace by cutting through white clouds.
Human life is rare to reach a full hundred years; why toil so bitterly in the competitive rush for profit and fame?
Having entered the mountains, I have learned to be simple and dull-witted; though I usually possess a mouth, I am too lazy to open it. Do not attempt to debate with those who are wrong;
you must surely prune away your own faults. The tile stove glows red as the tea is ready; white light fills the paper window as the moon first rises.
Through all time, who can understand this frivolous world? Only Yan Ling is permitted to sit upon his fishing platform.

The mountain stream is shallow and its spring water clear, revealing the stones and sand beneath; above the eaves, where no horns grow, vines and creepers take root. Deep in the night, under the moonlight, the long-voiced monkeys howl;

with thick moss covering the crags, few travelers pass before the cliffs. The bamboo in the courtyard leans as heavy spring snow falls; the plum blossoms on the ridge are withered by the many cold nights.
This Way is vast and empty, neither of this age nor of antiquity; it is in vain that one takes a brick and grinds it against a stone.
The white-haired Chan elder has long dwelt in his hermitage; His patched robe is wind-tossed and tattered. By the stream he sweeps leaves to fuel the hearth;
After the frost, bitter mugwort covers the tangerines. This original, innate nature is not a product of creation; This ready-made koan requires no further investigation.
With doors and windows wide open, he sits facing the courtyard; All day long he gazes at the mountains, never lowering the curtain.
Lying deep within the clouds, one does not face the court; One dwells merely by the wild waters of the layered cliffs. When returning from a dream upon the bamboo couch, the window holds the moon;
When the rice porridge is cooked in the earthen pot, there is no smoke from the hearth. All conditions have ceased, yet this is not through deliberate effort;
The single nature is perfectly luminous, inherently spontaneous. Profound as empty space, it is eternally unmoving; Let the vast ocean change into mulberry fields as it may.
In the meditation hall atop the peak, one rests upon a stone dais; white clouds fly away and then fly back again. Before the gate, a waterfall hangs suspended in the air and falls;

behind the house, mountain ridges rise like surging waves. On the plain walls, the Buddhas of the three periods are faintly sketched; in an earthenware vase, a branch of plum blossoms is steeped in fragrance.
Though the fields below are level and smooth, they cannot compare to this mountain home, free from even a speck of dust.
