The Great Way has never known waxing or waning from the start; yet those who do not understand it cling to expedient means.

While sages and worthies remain hidden in this age, false teachings circulate at this time. Lash your faculties with painful urgency and cease your self-indulgence; maintain right mindfulness constantly and do nothing else.
Once this human body is lost beneath the *kāṣāya*, ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes will not permit its recovery.

The dilapidated cottage stands desolate as I rest upon a stone terrace. For whom does the thatched gate open in broad daylight? In the arena of fame, crowds press shoulder-to-shoulder to enter; on the ancient road, no one comes to set foot.
In the deep night, cold with snow, there is only the fire-companion; at the fifth watch, chilled by frost, there is only the mournful cry of the ape.
The *kāṣāya* robe is tattered and hard to mend; I gather the clouds and mists to cut and tailor for myself.
The allotted span of human life is one hundred years; who among us can attain a full century?

Life is as precarious as a thatched roof leaning precariously, and as perilous as a leaking boat tossed upon the waves. The common practitioners of our time are truly to be pitied, and those who covet fame for their status as teachers are even more lamentable.
The ways of the world have declined from what they once were; day by day, I shall keep my wooden gate firmly shut.
Green mists and crimson clouds shroud the deep bamboo path; within a single hut, all day long it is cold and silent. To let go casually is to be without affairs;
yet to look with deliberate intent, there is still a mind. An ancient mirror, unpolished, contains the myriad phenomena; a great bell, struck once, emits its perfect sound.
This fundamental source-nature is the true-born Buddha—neither form nor emptiness, neither past nor present.
Leisurely and at ease, I sit in the home of a wild monk; Drinking and feeding as circumstances allow, I pass the years. Green bamboos and yellow flowers—this is my idle intent;
White clouds and flowing water—this is my simple life. Do not mistake a rock for a tiger in the mountains; Do not suspect a snake in the cup from the reflection of a bow.
Unaware of the affairs of the dusty world beneath the trees, I see the setting sun constantly escorting the homeward crows.
With a head full of white hair and a lean, skeletal frame, he is capable in every aspect of his daily livelihood. At the autumn equinox, he pounds white-arthroot in a wooden mortar;

at the midpoint of spring, he dries red-creeper in a bamboo basket. He buys yellow-rooted herbs from travelers before the mountain, and purple seaweed is constantly required from monks beyond the sea.
Who would say that at seventy-seven in the new year, he has opened a pond to plant lotus roots and water chestnuts?
The divination reveals deep crags far from the marketplace and court. The thatched gate is half-closed; the grasses rustle in the wind.
Who is it with white hair, poor yet free of flattery? Which one in a crimson gate, wealthy yet without pride? Urgent debts must not be settled through laxity;
delusive passions must be extinguished within stillness. Even the white clouds say the green mountains are good; night after night they fly there to accompany one’s solitude.
Wind-swept masts come and go, clogging the official canals; tethered horses gallop as if flying, bustling day and night.

Those who seek office out of a desire for favor and glory, and those who engage in commerce out of greed for life and profit—though human wealth and honor bring joy for a moment, the bitterness of hell endures for ten thousand kalpas.
From antiquity to the present, there is no medicine to cure this; why do you not go forth to practice the Way sooner?
Having entered this gate to study this school, one must scrutinize with utmost care and seek to fathom its depths. The essence of pure voidness and tranquil stillness remains;
when the calculating mind is forgotten, the objective realm is naturally empty. The trees hang with lingering clouds, a mass of white; the mountains embrace the setting sun, half crimson.
"Is it the wind that moves, or the banner? It is neither the banner, nor is it the wind.
The guest, loving its secluded stillness, arrives at the bamboo fence. Meeting [the monk], he realizes his own courtesy is utterly deficient. A mass of white hair hangs in disarray upon his head;

a single *kāṣāya* robe is worn in a haphazard fashion. After the fire has died out beneath the yellow leaves throughout the night, when the cries of the green monkeys have ceased at the fifth watch, they sit facing each other on their *pútuán* mats, embracing the pillow and forgetting words as they commune with this profound principle.
A hundred years of life pass like a horse's hoof in a crevice; how few reflect deeply upon this!

If the matter within one’s own person remains unclear, the shore of birth and death is truly perilous. The patchwork robe is the seamstress’s thread, the tears of a doting wife; fragrant rice is the old farmer’s sweat.
Do not say there is no cause and effect between giving and receiving; the cause exists, and the fruit will surely manifest in due time.
Since entering the mountains, ten thousand cares have cleared; with a single, level mind, I let things flow freely. The colors of the trees before my courtyard fade as autumn arrives;

the sound of the stream outside my railing increases after the rain. I gather wild chives and boil tea to entertain guests from the wilds; I buy pots and transplant chrysanthemums to send to the neighboring monk.
The sons of high officials, clad in brocade and feasting on jade-like delicacies, do not possess such sentiments as this mountain monk.

This body and its lifespan are like a bubble upon the water; one should simply pass through them with composure and let them be. When affairs do not accord with one's desires, there is always insufficiency;
if a person can take a step back, they will have no sorrow. Decline and prosperity are like the blooming and falling of flowers;
gathering and dispersing are just as clouds come and go. I have long since forgotten worldly thoughts; I remain slumped all day long, leaning against the peak tower.
I have realized for myself that my thoughts from past lives were light; now that I am old, I follow my natural course, delighting in leisurely sentiments.

With straw sandals and a bamboo staff in the third month of spring, I dream of paper curtains and plum blossoms at the fifth watch of the night. Seeking the Buddha or seeking immortality is entirely a deluded thought;
to be without worry and without anxiety is itself the practice of cultivation. Last night, the wind through the pines spoke with fervent clarity; it was simply that I, a deaf man, refused to listen.
Pass each day by following its course; why worry in advance for tomorrow? Life, death, aging, and illness cannot be predicted;
wealth, nobility, fame, and achievement do not remain long. Crimson gates by the lake are now entwined with creeping vines; paths by the mountain stream have turned into desolate mounds.
All that is spoken of concerns only the present moment, yet no one is willing to turn their head.
With white hair, the dhūta is beset by old age and illness; he has dwelt in his thatched hut for many years.

He has worn away innate attachments to ordinary sentiments, and now, through analytical dissolution, he follows the mind of sacred measure. A hundred birds do not come—the mountain is silent and still; ten thousand pines remain forever—deeply verdant and profound.
Clearly, this is the matter of the void kalpa beyond; a single divine light shines from antiquity to the present.
Vying for profit and rushing after fame—what is there to boast of? Only the wild monk’s household is permitted the leisure of purity.
In the field of the mind, weeds of ignorance do not grow; in the garden of awakening, the flowers of wisdom bloom forever. By the yellow earth mounds, bracken and bamboo shoots abound;
upon the ground of green moss, dust and sand are scarce. I came here when I was over thirty years old; how many times have clear windows reflected the setting glow of the sunset?

I am of the Chan school, yet I do not understand Chan. I find contentment beneath the forest trees to pass my remaining years. My patched robes, a hundred seams joined, hang over my entire body; three strips of bamboo rattan wind across my belly.
The colors of the mountains and the light of the stream reveal the Patriarch’s intent; the birds’ songs and flowers’ smiles awaken one to the conditions of the Dharma.
Sometimes I ascend alone to the flat rock on the terrace; at midnight, when there are no clouds, the moon fills the sky.

For over forty years I have lived in solitary seclusion; I know not how many cycles of prosperity and decline the dusty world has seen. At night, I burn pine needles in my hearth to ward off the cold;
at noon, I pluck wild vegetables to fill my bowl against hunger. Sitting upon rocks, I gaze at the clouds in moments of leisure; mending my robes in the morning sun is my practice of stillness.
Should anyone ask me for the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, I shall tell them everything I possess.
Vipers’ tails and wolfish hearts fill the world; everyone vies for precedence, each employing their own clever contrivances.
How many times can one laugh in a hundred years? Not even for a single moment does a day truly pass. When a carriage overturns, who knows to change its course?
When calamity arrives, there is no place to dwell in shame. This old monk does not speak with excessive verbosity; I wish only to strip away the veils and entanglements for all of you.
The sun and moon race on, never pausing for a moment; dwelling in the crags, I have suddenly reached the end of my years. My shadow grows ever thinner as I practice the Way by the ice;
my eyes turn a deeper blue as I gaze at the mountains from beneath the pines. Gathering fallen leaves, I fuel the earthen hearth; picking chrysanthemums in season, I place them in the bronze vase.
This toiling life is fond of drinking the wine of profit and fame; mired in stupor, there is no way to call oneself awake.
By the green waters and blue mountains, my thatched cottage has long served me well through the passing years.

A few trees of red and white peach and plum; a single field of green and yellow vegetables and wheat. On the bamboo couch at night, I sit listening to the rain; by the paper window in the clear weather, I sleep watching the clouds.
In human life, nothing surpasses the excellence of pure leisure. To attain such pure leisure—how could it be by mere chance?
The ancients entered the mountains for the sake of the Way; their daily practice was centered upon themselves. They added stones to their waists to grind white rice;
they carried hoes and planted pine trees in the rain. What harm is there in carrying mud and hauling stones?
What better use is there for one's effort than fetching water and moving firewood? Those who are indolent, seeking clothing and food—do not come to associate with this old Chan master.
The birth and growth of the myriad things are moved by their latent roots; whether one is long or another short need not be discussed. A mass of fierce fire is the path of profit and fame;
three feet of cold ice is the gate of Buddhas and Patriarchs. Grasses and brambles are the den of foxes; clouds and mists, the floating isle, are the realm of cranes.
With white hair filling my head, I dwell among the rocky valleys; how many times have I leaned upon the railing until the sun’s glow faded?

Dwelling in the crags was originally for the sake of cultivation; I did not permit others to know it, yet I constantly evaluated myself. My nature of the Way is pure and harmonious as residual habits have been exhausted;

the awakened mind is perfectly clear, the work of illumination accomplished. Planting pines and hoeing vegetables, my body remains robust; mending robes and translating sutras, my two eyes remain bright.
The times have changed and circumstances differ—how truly laughable! Though I fled Qin, I have nonetheless gained the name of one who hides in the mountains.
Having traversed the entire universe, I find no place to seek; by chance, I have come to dwell in these mountain forests.

My thatched hut rises high into the azure clouds, and mossy paths wind through the depths of bamboo and trees. Men are startled by profit, fame, honor, and disgrace; I, however, spend my years in the stillness of Chan meditation.
The ancient pines and strange rocks remain unrecognized by anyone; yet they still take their minds to search for the mind.
Old in years, my mind is at ease and my body is likewise; I sweep my single mat and lie beneath the pines.

Delighting in the profound stillness of this mountain retreat, I see how the world’s paths are treacherous and men grow ever more callous. The breeze is warm and the wild birds’ calls are shrill; the sun slants and the shadows of the flowering herbs fade away.
Wild herbs and millet are always available for our daily meals; there is no need to carry a bowl down the mountain again.
At dawn, drawing water, I open the wooden gate; I see the sky with all its mists withdrawn. The fragrance of yam fires stirs thoughts of idle gathering;
The peach blossoms have fallen, awakening me to the Cloud of Spirit. Monkeys and cranes in the woods are sights long familiar; The world’s decline and prosperity are sounds unheard.
How many times I have sat until the mossy stone grew warm; These fine mountains I gaze upon until the slanting glow of dusk.
In the depths of white clouds, I have built a thatched hut; my simple livelihood brings more than enough joy. Before I die, I shall keep the fire for warming the roots;
why must one write letters of severance to end worldly ties? Tranquil and still, it penetrates the three periods of time; vast and perfectly luminous, it envelops the ten directions of space.
Within the hermitage, one knows nothing of what lies beyond; how many times have the flowers fallen and bloomed again?
Examine minutely the nature of ephemeral things; victory and defeat are difficult to determine in a single game of chess. It is only when dwelling among green peaks that a monk finds true leisure;

when one is amidst the red dust of the world, old age comes before one realizes it. As the wind stirs tea-smoke rising from the bamboo couch, and water carries falling petals to the green pond—how can one allow the thirty-six thousand days of life to pass without letting the body and mind rest in stillness for even a brief moment?
Thus, go with such thoroughness; let go and let it all fall away from the beginning. Two lips gather white mold; an ancient path grows long with moss.
A wooden horse flies like lightning at the edge of the clouds; a clay ox bellows like thunder at the bottom of the sea.
When snow covers ten thousand peaks on a clear moonlit night, the scent of spring arrives in secret upon the cold plum blossoms.
Pure poverty is the path of eternal joy for the man of the Way; in every daily activity, all things naturally harmonize.
Last night the western wind blew through the ancient trees; at dawn the ground was covered with dry firewood. Clouds drift like white silk, clinging to the vermilion walls;
dewdrops fall like pearls, adorning the green cliffs. One’s livelihood has always followed the present moment; there is no need to laboriously arrange it.
Clearly and constantly aware, yet appearing as if unaware; carefree and detached, like a pillar or a fool. Turning heaven and overturning mountains, forever abiding in stillness;
a single thought lasts ten thousand years, never shifting. With ears, one hears sounds like wind passing through trees; with no-mind, one responds to things like the moon reflecting in a pond.
Do not say that only I alone can understand this clearly; every person is capable of doing it.
My schemes are clumsy; I am ashamed that my talent for engaging with the world is deficient. Though possessed of intelligence, I have no share in it, being as dull-witted as a fool.

I say to myself that all objects and environments are empty illusions; who can understand that wealth and resources are all but fleeting arrivals? Yellow leaves drift with the current, coming and going at leisure;
white clouds hang across the valley, wandering aimlessly. It is only when both eyes are closed that things are truly well; yet out of love for the green mountains, they are opened once more.
With a shaven head and square-cut robes, one becomes a śramaṇa; thus one encounters the descendants of the Muni Buddha. Ceasing evil and warding off wrongdoing, one tames the horse of the mind;
forgetting contrivance and stilling views, one restrains the monkey of the heart. Refining the demonic through the nature of the Way, the true gold is purified;
nurturing the source of spirit, the fine jade is warm. One cannot lead another by the hand; only when one is willing themselves will they become intimate.
The crimson sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night; the evening bell tolls as the cock crows at the fifth watch. Heaven and earth have aged me until my hair is white with snow;
the passing years have worn away a hundred jars of pickled vegetables. Borrowing the ground to plant pines for future rafters, I eat peaches and spit out the pits, which grow into a grove.
To those on this world who are like fledglings wounded by an arrow, I say: it is best to seek a tree to nest in deep within the mountains.
The Way of the Dharma is vast and silent, beyond imitation; a deep seclusion in a single hermitage is a worthy plan. Before the gate, bamboo grows tall enough to shade the house;
from the rocks, spring water is divided to flow directly into the kitchen. Monkeys bring their young as fruit ripens on the cliffs; cranes move their nests away as pines wither by the stream.
Amidst the stillness of Zen, there is much leisurely sentiment: gathering dry firewood to tend the earthen stove.
How little remains of the fleeting light of this world? Who can avoid this ceaseless rushing from wave to wave? When the kitchen is empty, one must go out to seek the yellow tubers;

when the patched robe is torn, one thinks of cutting green lotus leaves for mending. The fly-whisk is laid aside and speech is cut off; the Buddhist sutras are forgotten, and the bookworms within them multiply.
Piteous indeed is the state of one dwelling beneath the *kāṣāya*, yet chasing after sensory objects and clinging to conditions like hemp seeds on a flax field.

Pentasyllabic Regulated Verse The practitioner’s conditioned thoughts have ceased; Everything encountered by the eye is the radiance of the mind. Where does the blue peach blossom wither? Fragrance fills the flowing waters of the stream.
The grass grows deep and the snake’s nature rejoices; The sun is warm and the butterfly’s heart grows wild. I once heard an old woodcutter say: "Beyond the clouds lies the chamber of Zhizhou."
A single mattock suffices for a lifetime; this is the home of one who dwells on the mountain path. Having work, I plant only bamboo; having no leisure, I do not cultivate flowers.
At night, water-mills pound rice; in spring, bamboo baskets bake tea. Where in the human world am I? Faintly, I see the mulberry and hemp.
From time to time I smile to myself; in old age I have found peace and leisure. Within my heart there is nothing at all; before my eyes there are only mountains.
Under the vast sky, the Peng bird spreads its wings; in heavy mist, the leopard’s spots grow more distinct. Only the plum blossom is my friend; we shall keep our promise through the coldest year.
All myriad conditions have come to rest; in a single thought, center and periphery are severed. All day long one remains in leisurely ease; for years on end, one dwells in tranquility.

The mountains are empty and the clouds move freely; the sky is clear and the moon is solitary and full. When the work of refinement reaches its consummation, it cannot be equated with the Zen of intellectual understanding.

From this rocky terrace, my gaze extends across the wild landscape; faintly visible is the pine-clad gate. This was a temple for eminent monks of the Tang dynasty, now the tomb of a Prime Minister from the Song.

The light of the stream pours far away in the clear weather, while the colors of the wilds grow dim as evening falls. The songs on the mountain paths have ceased; woodcutters return to their smoke-filled villages.
Winding paths of yellow mud, circular fences of purple hibiscus; Paper windows open in bamboo huts, tile stoves burning pine branches.
In this state of plain simplicity where the mind is forgotten, In this desolate moment when all illumination has ceased— Who else can be like me? Without affairs, and without action.
The dwelling place of a monk in the deep mountains is truly superior to Penglai. Upon the ground there is no grass; within the garden, however, there are plum blossoms.

When idleness is abundant, all discursive thoughts are extinguished; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the mind opens of itself. A single worn-out patchwork robe is spread out upon the stone platform to dry in the clouds.
A gust arises from nowhere; its whistling pervades the nine realms. It makes the forest trees tremble and blows my bamboo gate open.
Fundamentally formless from the start, how could there be coming or going? Seeking the ultimate limit, one cannot reach it; a tiger laughs upon the rocky terrace.

At the summit of the mountain, mists and vapors gather; by the clouds’ edge, a small cottage peeks out. Cool in summer with windows near the bamboo, warm in winter as the pavilion faces the morning sun.
Silk garments from cocoon paper are soft; mountain fields offer fragrant gruel and rice. This life passes according to its lot; there is nothing left to ponder.
A single hoe suffices for one’s livelihood; for many years, one is satiated by water and firewood. With mountains worthy of gazing upon, there is no worldly affair to trouble the heart.
Mist and wind moisten the thatched cottage; moss marks ascend the earthen steps. Following conditions as they arise ultimately saves effort;

there is truly no need for contrivance. In the mountain kitchen, the midday offering is prepared; the spring water is white like silver syrup. The soup is cooked with tender bamboo shoots; the rice is steamed from fragrant non-glutinous grain.
Fried in oil, the *qingding* mushroom; boiled in vinegar, the purple sprout ginger—none of the hundred flavors can equal these; what need is there to speak of those from the higher realms?

The absolute void is like a tranquil sea; the slightest movement creates a bubble. As soon as one receives the retribution of a physical form, one immediately harbors anxieties regarding food and clothing.
Consciousness and emotion gallop like wild horses; deluded thoughts run like mad monkeys. Failing to realize the intent of the King of Emptiness, the cycle of rebirth will not cease.
In the eighth month of the mountain home, the season and its objects naturally harmonize: fresh bean pods hang from the ridges, and the fragrance of rice fills the fields.
I cut reeds to repair my old cottage, and hew bamboo to find a clear spring. Who in this world knows me? I wander freely, enjoying my later years.
Amidst the thatched hut and bamboo trees, I have no concern with the dusty world. My gate faces a single pool of water; my windows open onto mountains on all four sides.
Smoke has blackened the tea stove; dampness has stained the coarse woolen robe. Failing to realize the Dharma of the Empty King, for what reason have I attained this leisure?
The crimson sun half-swallows the mountain; the wooden gate is then closed. Green rushes serve as a soft mat; the white wood pillow is curved.
The moon over the pines comes first to shine; the clouds from the stream emerge but do not yet return. My long journey through the clear night’s dream refuses to enter the world of men.

Cane in hand, I emerge from the pine forest; walking with measured steps, I ascend the verdant peaks. A flock of cranes scatters as they encounter hawks; the shadows of trees fall into the sinking stream.

Wild fruits are difficult to gather due to thorns; medicinal sprouts are easy to find for their fragrance. With light mist and the slanting rays of setting sun, scarlet leaves cover half the rock’s shadow.
Of thousands upon thousands of fine peaks, the dwelling occupies the highest tier. Three Buddha statues have been simplified in form; a single bowl of lamp remains perpetually lit.
The bell tolls through the cold night moon; tea brews upon the ice of the stone pond. When a guest asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, I can only say: "I am unable.
In taking and rejecting, in acting and withdrawing—each person in life has their own way. Heaven and earth allow me my indolence; fame and profit make others busy.
Gulls sleep on the banks with their backs to the sun; swallows build nests circling the rafters. Sentiment is deluded, turning along with external things;

one cannot realize the King of Emptiness. Binding grass, they make a hut; year after year it is covered with thatch. The paper windows are darkened by pine needles; the bamboo house is plastered with moss.
Barley rice requires only a little fire; wild herb soup needs not a pinch of salt. My life passes according to my lot; who cares for the world’s disdain? A Seven-Character Quatrain:
In the chilly thatched cottage on a new autumn night, White bean flowers bloom as the cricket cries. The mountain moon, like silver, draws the old man [into his dreams].
While wandering at leisure, I did not realize I had passed the western peak.

The mountains are full of bamboo shoots and bracken; the gardens are full of tea plants. A single tree bears red blossoms interspersed with white ones. Generally, spring is the best of the four seasons;
yet among them, the mountain home is most excellent.
Someone asked me how many years I have lived here; it was only after sitting for a long time that I realized:
I personally planted the green peach trees outside my gate, and the spring light has seen them bloom twenty times.
Weary of toil and labor, one loves peace and leisure. How can such a person dwell in the mountains?
Before Baizhang’s time, those who lived in mountain caves made their entire livelihood from the side of their mattock.
In my old age, I dwell in a hermitage to nurse my ailing body; though the sun has risen high, I have not yet opened the door. Fearing the cold, I rise from my seat to kindle pine fires;
the sound of a woodcutter’s song reaches me from across the valley.

The youth has never stirred a fire since arriving; clouds and rain have already come to provide for his midday meal. In this mountain hermitage, he rejoices in being exempt from taxes and corvée labor;
he plants nothing but pine trees, selling only firewood.
In the Jade Hall, beneath silver candles, the night resounds with song and laughter; in the Golden Valley, within silken curtains, dwell the houses of wealth and honor.
How can these compare to the hermit beneath his thatched hut, where under a clear sky and bright moon, the plum blossoms bask in the light?
Wherever we meet, all speak of the hardships of the world; each seeks restlessness within their own hermitage.
Were it not for Yuanming’s "Returning Home," there would be not a single person willing to resign from office.

The mountain kitchen is silent, the smoke of cooking cut off; frozen locks the sound of the spring on this day that longs for snow. The old monk facing the wall lacks the power of meditative concentration;
once again he thinks of begging for food among the people of the world.
Having finished planting the winter melons, one then plants the eggplants; toiling the body and exhausting the bones as one’s livelihood.
If everyone wishes for the kitchen to be well-supplied, the head gardener must always remain at home.
When will the cycle of porridge gone and rice coming to an end? When will the rising of the sun and the setting of the moon cease?
In truth, these have no concern for me; they are but idle thoughts arising in vain.
Behind the house stand eight or nine pine trees; before the gate, two or three furrows of purple yams. The mountain-dwelling practitioner has few worldly schemes;
he speaks of his household fires from beginning to end to others.
Who would dare to force this matter? Unless one knows that there is [something], one cannot know it. It is clear that the moon is upon the plum blossoms;
by the time you see the blossoms, it is already too late.
Past matters have already passed away; there is no need to anticipate or deliberate about the future. Speak directly right now—this very phrase:
when the plum ripens, the *kakkola* flower is fragrant.

One day, one strikes sleep three or five times; even this cannot exhaust so much idleness. Circling several times through the *lang-zhan* bamboo, once again one emerges among the green pines to gaze at the distant mountains.
Grasping at conditions and arising from inversion are easily dispelled; it is sudden urgency that makes love and hate difficult to eliminate. I laugh at the green mountains, so lofty and abrupt;
the green mountains resent me for my gauntness as I climb their tiers.
The true void is profoundly still and eternally present; yet the fertile field of consciousness is unwittingly obscured by delusion. How could true nature ever depart from illusory existence?
Flowers bloom and fall of their own accord in the spring breeze.
The waters of Heaven Lake are as deep and clear as lapis lazuli; misty clouds and mountains surround it like a brocade screen of red. All that meets the eye is a reality already manifest;
why need one join the palms to question an elder in meditation?
In old age my vigor has declined; I am truly indolent. At dawn, I no longer even offer a greeting. When guests arrive, I have no words with which to respond;
they labor in vain to reach this thatched hut.
In my old age, my entire being is but indolence; when at leisure, all hundred thoughts turn to ashes. Meeting with you, my brother, was but a mere snap of the fingers;
yet, helpless against human sentiment, I must join you in forced company.
The fields are free of dust and have not been swept for long; the thatched gate opens only when a guest knocks. The snow has cleared and the slanting moon pierces the eaves with its chill;
the shadow of a single branch of plum falls upon the window.
A thatched cottage, lowly and consisting of only three or two rooms, is encircled on all sides by green mountains. The bamboo bed allows no lingering clouds to lodge;
before the sun has even slanted, the door is already closed.
What brings you, my Zen brother, to this misty thicket? My old life’s sustenance is meager indeed. Beneath the crags, the osmanthus fills the trees with fragrance;
in the garden, the sprouts of vegetables have formed green clusters.
A single expanse of dustless ground after fresh rain; half a slope of ancient pines covered in moss.
All people see these sights before their eyes, yet who knows that their ways of utilizing them differ?
The myriad realms and myriad conditions are all stilled; every single cognition and perception is entirely dissolved. Leisurely, both ears have no further use;
one sits until the dawn cock and the evening bell.
The mountain cave is silent and still all day long; worldly thoughts have never had so much as a hair’s breadth here.
Though one wears clothes and eats porridge and rice, it is just as if one were dead and has not yet been cremated.
A newly sewn paper quilt, warmed by the sun, brings a peaceful sleep until the fifth watch.
Hearing the bells and drums of the upper realm strike, yet another day is added to this fleeting life.
A withered tree before the gate stands like a person; A fine mountain behind the house rises like a mass of waves. An old man like me has nothing more to say to you:
The high path of clouds has deceived you, my brother, into coming here.
The mountain shapes are undulating and the paths rise and fall; stones occupy the treetops and houses the footpaths.
The land is so narrow that there is little room for growing vegetables, so another small garden has been established to the west of the bridge.
Hundreds of thousands of days and nights pass within; eighty thousand afflictions are extinguished in stillness. Amidst the radiance of green waters, mountain shadows shift;
upon the flames of a red furnace, snowflakes drift.
There is a road to the West, yet one is unwilling to go; though hell has no gate, they struggle to pass through it. The immortal maidens are small in the golden pavilions and silver towers;
the sinners are many in the cauldrons and burning furnaces.
When you direct your mind to seek the Truth, the Truth moves ever further away; when you apply your heart to sever delusion, delusion remains all too abundant.
For the practitioner who dwells in a single state of equanimity, the moon is in the blue sky while its reflection is in the waves.
To aspire to become a Buddha is truly easy; Only to sever the deluded mind is truly difficult.
Through many nights of frosty skies and bright moonlight, I sit until dawn and realize the chill of the fifth watch.
All conditions having been cast off, the mind is free from affairs; all phenomena being empty, the nature is serene. How many times has the moon at the empty window poured forth its white light?
The moon and the flowing water reach the very gate.
When there is no mind regarding a single thing, all things come to rest; then there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Do not say that being without mind means there are no matters at all, for there still remains the very thought of "no-mind."
With no mind toward phenomena, it is like wind passing through trees; with no phenomena within the mind, it is like the moon moving through the sky.
When the sound of the wind and the color of the moon have been entirely worn away, one layer is cast off only to reveal another.
The head of the new year and the tail of the old. Tomorrow is the fourth and today is the third. My spiritual practice remains unaccomplished as my hair turns white;
throughout the great trichiliocosm, there is nowhere to hide my shame.
White hair hastens one’s emaciation until it reaches the shoulders; I have lived in this thatched hut for many years. My trousers lack waistbands and my leggings have no openings;
this single tunic is missing half its length.

I have not yet finished reading this single scroll of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The slanting shadows of the setting sun flow eastward with the water. The clouds return to their own place and take up lodging beneath the thatched eaves;
another day’s span of time has already come to an early end.
Rain falls upon the thatched eaves, then the sun turns crimson; in an instant, the weather shifts from gloom to clarity.
How much more so for the matter of life and death, which hangs on a breath—how can one be certain at twilight to hear the morning bell?
Clearly seeing is not the seeing of another; clearly knowing is always knowing without a separate knower.
I remember last autumn, amidst the rain and mist, a monkey came and stole away a pair of pears.
Half a window of pine shadows, half a window of moonlight; a single meditation cushion, a single monk.
Having sat cross-legged since deep into the night, a moth has flown in and extinguished the lamp before the Buddha.
For many years my mind has been entirely free of concerns; each day within my hermitage, my joy is more than sufficient.
After finishing my meal, I brew a strong tea and drink it, then sit upon a stone by the pond and count the swimming fish.
Five *he* of aged yellow millet are steamed for rice; several stalks of green shepherd’s purse sprouts are boiled for soup. Its simple flavor is naturally delicious;
why should one need to add more ginger or pepper?
My family has moved deep into the western mountains; layers upon layers of misty trees separate us from the distant stream. In my old age, my mind is at ease and I crave the stability of sleep;
I am weary of hearing the tolling of bells and the crowing of roosters.
The mountain wind blows through the old window paper; Flakes of snow fly in one by one. Though I layer my cloth robes to their full, they offer no warmth at all;
I gather dry wood and dig deep into the ashes of the earthen stove.
Slanting sunlight through half-open windows casts a cool glow; Clad in tattered robes, he sits with his head covered upon a bamboo bed. Withered leaves fill the hearth as the flames burn;
He knows not that frost lies cold upon the roof above.
How many mountain trees bear blossoms red and brilliant; a single pool of spring water ripples with green waves.
If a patch-robed monk possesses eyes that transcend the school, he need not wait for insentient things to trigger his awakening.
Before the clouds have returned, I close the door; on my rustic bed, I sleep soundly in profound stillness. In this mountain home, neither chicken nor dog is raised;
when the sun reaches the thatched eaves, my dream has not yet awakened.
The congee is gone and the rice has arrived; having finished my tea, I open the window and sit alone gazing at the green mountains.
Carefully calculating the billions of Jambudvīpa worlds, there is no one in all this bright day as idle as I.
The black mist and thick clouds cannot be parted; suddenly gone, suddenly come. Let their wiles perish of themselves;
the red sun shines as before upon the stone terrace.
One day, as the red sun rose in the southeast, he plucked green seedlings himself to plant in the lean fields. His robe was half-saturated with mud and water;
returning home, he took it off to dry before his bamboo cottage.
I ate a peach and spat out the pit; the pit became a tree. The tree grew large, flowers bloomed, and peaches formed again.
How many times have spring passed and autumn come? Why should I not have white hair?
The thatched cottage is but a single zhang square—how stingy! Four eaves of pines and bamboos, surrounded on all sides by mountains. Even for this old monk to dwell here, it is already cramped;
how could it allow the clouds to come and borrow half a room?
When facing the opportune moment, by all means do not avoid the sword and spear; resolve to die and fight him one battle.
Once the barrier of Zhaozhou is broken through, throughout the great thousand-fold world-system there is nowhere that does not submit.
The finite span of time is but one hundred years; how few attain a full century? Even if one lives a hundred years, in the end one returns to death;
it is merely the division of what comes after from what came before.
The entire great treasury of the canon is but worn-out scrap paper; the seventeen hundred volumes are nothing but nests of entanglements.
Who can go and seek their clear understanding? Even to give rise to a single thought is already too much.
Yellow leaves by the stream drift with the water’s flow; white clouds upon the ridge come and go with the wind.
How can these compare to this old monk, ever unmoving, sitting year after year without concern upon his rocky dais?
The path to Mount Xiawu is high and the road is far. My hermitage is secluded, lacking even the three main paths. Yet I find my dwelling too perilous;
it has deceived many, causing them the toil of climbing.
Aging, I perceive my form withered and my strength declined; when guests arrive, I must strain myself to come forth and attend them. I pity myself for not knowing how to conceal my traces;
eating pine needles and wearing lotus robes, I long for the time at Damei.
The hermit’s dwelling is cold, with bamboo at its four eaves; the elder’s gate is high, with walls a hundred feet tall. The hermit’s heart grows ever more tranquil as the house grows cold;
the elder is increasingly busy as the gate grows high.
The common way holds that the ordinary mind is not Buddha-nature; I say that Buddha-nature is precisely the ordinary mind.
In practice, one only fears that no one will do it—grind an iron pestle until it becomes a needle for thread.
Going and returning to the south, north, east, and west; traveling by carriage and horse on land, by boat upon the water.
The paths to profit and fame are as distant as the heavens, driving thousands upon thousands of people in this world to their ruin.
How can one find the true opportunity while dwelling in the mountains? Having planted the winter melon, one then plants the gourd.
Should even a hair’s breadth of effort fail to reach it, these vast fields will all fall into ruin.
Having been away from the assembly for many years, I have had no sitting mat; having entered the mountains for a long time, my kashaya robe has worn away.
I am left with nothing but a single iron cauldron, kept here to boil the spray of the waterfall for whoever may come.
Wearing coarse cloth with tattered seams and sowing green hemp, they harvest early rice whenever grain is scarce.
Through bitter toil, they provide mending and support so that you may remain free from debt and repay your benefactors.

Rice is fragrant when mixed with parched wheat flour and pine powder; the vegetables are excellent when blended with wisteria blossoms and bamboo shoots. Having reached the end of my life, I have no other thoughts:
let him [the Buddha] become a Buddha or be reborn in heaven as he pleases.

The livelihood of one dwelling in the mountains lies at the edge of the mattock. Clothing and food must be provided; they do not come of themselves. One plants rice in the fields until the mud reaches the knees;
one carries firewood out to the market with shoulders strained by the pole.
An iron-tipped mattock hangs from the eaves of the house; when vigorous, one clears the clouds, when weary, one sleeps. At the zenith of the red sun, the yam ripens;
its sweet fragrance does not lie by the hearth.
A single round hut with a pointed roof; who outside would know its interior is so spacious?
It accommodates the entire great trichiliocosm, yet there remains idle ground to place a meditation cushion.
A thatched hut is built amidst tall pine trees; on every side, the windows and screens are wide open. Facing the green mountains, I sit all day long;
not a single thing arises to disturb the mind.
In the deep autumn season, the rain falls in fine drizzle; Layers of moss leaves bear the imprints of tiger’s paws. An evening west wind blows without ceasing;
At dawn, yellow leaves reach the level of the steps.
The round red sun rises over the green mountains; the bamboo cottage and wooden gate remain shut.
The white-haired old monk has not yet risen from sleep, while the toil of life circles like ants upon a grindstone.
The mountain cottage is pure and secluded, utterly free from a speck of dust; with a mind at ease, it naturally distinguishes itself from the world.
One knows not where the azure peach has blossomed, yet a solitary bird brings it here, circling the bamboo gate.
In old age, there is nothing to trouble the mind; on my bamboo couch, I sleep high with the sun slanting upon my pillow. In dreams, I know not who I am;
when I awaken, the new moon has reached the plum blossoms.
After meditation, I chant the verses of Hanshan aloud; after the meal, I brew strong Guyu tea.
Still having leisurely feelings with nowhere to be placed, I carry my basket over the ridge to gather wisteria flowers.
Because monastics possess productive lands, they are burdened with tax levies; when government officials summon them for collection, their shame and humiliation are great.
I have three and a half mu of mountain fields, which I now offer in their entirety to the *dānapati*.
At Chuge Ge, the incense burner is set and charcoal is piled; the bed is spread with fresh mats and new cotton quilts. How can one describe this warmth and vitality throughout the winter?
In dreams, one does not even think of Tuṣita Heaven.
Last year the household fire lacked support; this year the household fire shall not suffer want. In the fields there is a bountiful harvest of three pecks of grain;
at the gate a square pond has been added.
A peaked-roofed hut amidst the shadows of white clouds; a broken-legged cauldron atop a heap of yellow leaves. A leaking sieve stirs up rice-less gruel;
a cracked sand-pot pounds raw ginger to a pulp.
How could one who practices not attain Buddhahood? A drop of water wears away stone over many years. It is not that the hard skin cannot be pierced;
it is only that people lack the firmness of their own minds.
Sitting alone, the mind is exhausted; it is silent and profound. Within this, there is no dharma that can withstand the heart’s inquiry.
The west wind has blown away the leaves crowding the gate, leaving only the empty steps for the moonlight to shine upon.
Jade butterflies and plum blossoms fill the trees with fragrance; in the pond, greens washed for vegetables float upon the green surface.
If the young master in his brocade robes were to understand this, he would surely move his household to dwell among the *bìluó* vines.

Whether in adversity or prosperity, one never forgets this Way; in success or failure, it is all of one flavor, for everything is believed to be prior conditions. This is the thorough realization of the nature of space;
without moving a single hair’s breadth, it is fundamentally natural.
In the cold, I wear garments of lotus leaves for warmth; when hungry, I eat pine blossoms, fragrant as cakes and pastries.
Unlike worldly people who toil for the sake of mouth and body, I spend my life without rushing south or north in haste.
The newly sewn paper quilt is warm and steaming; amidst the heap of yellow leaves, the fire burns a brilliant red. Lost in idle dreams, I know not who has awakened me;
at the fifth watch, I hear the bell from below.
I hew green firewood and carry it away bundle by bundle; I must guard against it slipping from my shoulder, keeping it no higher than my waist. Today’s life does not guarantee tomorrow’s sun;
let me first finish burning through this night at the cold hearth.
This year’s weather is unfathomable; in a single day, the sky shifts from sun to rain several times. Beneath the eaves, the paper windows dry and then grow damp again;
by the front gate, the stone path becomes wet and then dries once more.
The mountain peak is entirely covered with pines in every direction. A thatched cottage sits nestled within the shade of the trees. From where does a gust of celestial wind arise?
It stirs up waves and billows that resound through the half-vault of the sky.
A yellow silk robe and a purple *kāṣāya*— when entering and leaving the gates of nobles and finding favor— how can these compare to the practitioner who forgets both honor and disgrace,
mending his lotus-leaf garment with pine needles and willow threads?
Spring has returned and summer faded, now comes the cool of autumn. The sun's shadow passes like a shuttle as the nights grow longer. One spends all one's effort in idle chatter;
how often does one turn back for even a moment’s reflection?
I observe that people of this age are busy day and night, extensively building houses and establishing estates;
yet at the end, they can take nothing with them—only their skulls are buried on Mount Beimang.
Everyone knows and hears of birth and death; why do you not practice cultivation early? The grand and majestic Great Way—no one reaches it;
with eyes wide open and clear-sighted, you fall straight into a fire pit.

To speak exhaustively, the practice of cultivation does not lie in delay. This life is followed by the prospect of future lives; yet within the three miserable realms, a single retribution lasts for five thousand kalpas.
Once one has emerged from there, when will it truly be?
The famous Geyamoku-sen in Kagawa Province is a celestial lake. I recall first settling there at the beginning of the Renzi year.
Upon the mountain peak lies a flat stone slab, resembling a blue lotus emerging from the water. Furthermore, there is the spring of Tenko; from antiquity until today, how... [it has remained].
Once withered, he settled by a spring and built a hut, intending to spend his final years there. Not a speck of red dust lay upon his grounds;

though the exterior appearance seemed narrow, the interior space was vast and spacious. Green gauze like mist veiled the golden image; carved trays and *chen-shui* incense rose toward the celestial path.
Meditation cushions and Zen chairs were arranged left and right; fragrant bells and cloud-shaped gongs rang at dawn and dusk. Earthenware jars...
The soil grows auspicious *kuśa* grass; stone basins and dragon pools nurture *pǔ* reeds. The rice from mountain fields makes fragrant gruel and smooth porridge;

melons are sweet and vegetables tender—these are the greens of one’s own garden. Cast aside gain and loss, right and wrong; walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are no longer bound by constraints.
At times he holds a white fly-whisk; at times he carries a string of blackwood beads. At times he dances with a joyful body;
at times he sits in silence like a *cīr̥ḍa* bird. He is too weary to raise the intent of the Patriarchs who came from the West; what need is there to speak of the poetry and books of the East?
I myself do not know whether these are ordinary people or sages; how could others possibly distinguish between oxen and donkeys? Guests arrive, yet I have no leisure to engage them in conversation;
I gather withered wood first to fuel the tea stove. The fragrant red blossoms unfold in spring; the cool shade is lush and dense as the summer trees spread like a veil.
The rock-orchids call out before the wind, returning the valley to life; the plum blossoms amidst the snow are truly pure and refined.
Lin Pu: There is no such true joy in the human world; what danger or anxiety could there be within the mountains? I do not take pleasure in his light carriage and high canopy;
I do not take pleasure in his leading a multitude or managing a following; I do not take pleasure in his Western Land of Ultimate Bliss;
nor do I take pleasure in his Pure Abodes in the heavens. In my heart, I am always free from insufficiency; in all that meets my eyes, I find abundance. The night lutes...
Music harmonizes; at dawn, the sun rises like a crow. Playful fish leap and frolic; fine birds call to one another.

The path leads through the profound and the remote; the realm transcends the world in its purity and emptiness. Poets exhaust their thoughts yet cannot compose a verse; artists employ every ingenuity yet cannot paint a picture.
Only Yuanming could truly inspire me, for he understood to say, "I too love my thatched cottage. He dwelt within the mountains until his passing.
In my leisure time, no one understands; I know only myself. I circle the mountain driving bamboo pipes for cold water, strike stones to take fire and prolong the morning cooking.
Fragrant rice is pounded as soon as it is harvested, and firewood is felled as soon as it is needed. Before the sand pot even boils, my saliva already drips in anticipation.
Before the slash-and-burn fields have been sown with purple taro, I must further plant yellow millet. By day, my hands and feet find no rest; by evening, [the work is not yet done].
When my divine thoughts grew weary, I returned home, washed my feet, and climbed onto my bed to sleep. So overcome by exhaustion, I did not notice the mountain moon shifting;
only when a solitary bird suddenly called from across the forest was I awakened. A ball of red sun hung from the pine branches. Today and tomorrow shall be thus;
next year and the year after shall be just so. Spring grasses grow lush and tall; summer trees flourish with verdant foliage; autumn clouds drift in scattered fragments; winter snows fall.
Mist and spray. The void falls to earth and Mount Sumeru shatters; the Tathāgatas of the three periods cast off their robes of defilement.
In clear brightness, they ascend the peaks of the clouds without contention. Stretching their brows, they gaze to the furthest reaches, opening the heart’s chest.

Ten thousand acres of Lake Tai shimmer with white waves; the two points of Lake Dongting are a blur of green mist. At first, one suspects these are immortals beginning to bind their topknots, wearing hats of emerald gauze.
The screen was lowered. Again, I suspected that a heavenly maiden had come to offer flowers; she presented two lotuses upon a jade platter.
Knowing clearly that this realm is entirely illusory and false, my mind remained at ease before it, yet its longing was not yet ended. I lingered about, unable to bear returning immediately;
the evening sun had already shifted behind the pines on the mountain peak.
The male magpie cries "jue" beside the eaves; the crow circles the house with its "ya-ya" call. A practitioner from Xianan Temple comes to deliver fruit;
a young child from the eastern neighbor goes to steal melons. Since the divination of omens and signs is thus proven effective, the retribution for sins and blessings must likewise be without error.
If a practitioner holds such views, then blemishes will appear upon the surface of the bronze mirror. Upon seeing this, Lanrong [was struck].
After the Fourth Patriarch passed away, the hundred birds no longer came to carry off flowers;
the forest trees grew ever-new leaves, casting much cool shade around the cottage. Deep grasses swallowed the traces of dust, and across the mountains one could hear the songs of woodcutters.
I plow my own land and sow my own seeds; with my hat tilted and a green raincoat draped over me, may the good rain come in its season to nourish my newly planted rice.
I cast my gaze across the universe, seeing that every single thing is subject to decay. Since I have well understood the principle of emptiness, how could I not find joy in returning to this state?
Hanshan once spoke these words: "My mind is like the autumn moon. I too have spoken these words: "My mind surpasses the autumn moon.
The autumn moon is not without brilliance, yet it waxes and wanes. How can it compare to my mind, which is perfectly bright and eternally pure?
Someone asked how the mind is; I was instructed on how to speak:
"The moon comes to shine upon my gate; The wind comes to blow upon my breast. I urge you to sit upon the rock, And listen to my mountain chant."
The dark hair has turned to white snow; the morning light has become evening gloom. All things are like dew upon the tips of blades of grass—how could they remain forever as they are now?
Having eaten my fill, I embrace a stone and sleep; when my sleep is done, I rise to wander idly. The scenery of early summer is vast and serene; in the new trees, yellow orioles sing.
Looking up and down, I dally with the things of the season; relaxed and unrestrained, I let my poetic sentiments flow. This alone is true joy; why must one seek empty fame?

On a small scale, I have not read the Buddhist scriptures; on a large scale, I do not understand the profound essence. How could I know that the hundred thousand gates of truth reside within this very square inch of the heart?
All day long you indulge in greed and anger; when will you contemplate birth and death? Once old age and sickness arrive, your regrets will be in vain.
You plant beans in two or three rows, which grow lushly across the field; unaware of the power of the spring warmth, you speak only of the strength of the soil.
An old rabbit crouches at the foot of a cliff, heart and mind filled with longing. If the fruit can truly satisfy your greed, I would rather go without sauce.
A single rain nourishes the mountains; all things upon the plains flourish. By planting three mu of yams by hand, one may even prolong the evening meal.
Alas, the people of this world! Fame and profit are ever locked within their bosoms. Snow falls thick upon their heads, while dust swirls vast within their chests.
They build huts on the peaks of desolate mountains and pass day and night according to conditions. Returning from selling firewood or selling rice, they cook porridge and prepare meals to eat.
Although this involves wearying the physical frame, it at least spares one from the labor of household service. Yet, when the wondrous is explained and the profound discussed, no one understands it.
Let go completely; let go entirely. Do not even attempt to be a Buddha. A single movement of thought becomes a demon; a single opening of the mouth invites calamity.
Drinking and pecking, I simply follow conditions; thus I pass my days in leisurely ease. To grasp at dharmas and practice cultivation is like bringing an ox to pull a millstone.
With a broken house of but three or two rafters, I dwell atop a thousand peaks. As the clouds disperse and the sky becomes clear and vast, I cast my gaze out to look around at will.
The world is like flowers in the empty sky; their arising and ceasing are all illusory and false. As the sun sets behind the mountains and the wind grows cold, I close my door and burn fire within.
I have built a hut atop a misty peak, where plowing and weeding are my daily tasks. My mountain fields number six or seven plots, and there are two or three practitioners here.
Digging a pond to let the moonlight in; selling firewood and buying rice to get by. This old man has few clever tricks; his private affairs have all been laid bare.
Two poor practitioners of the Way, three leaky and dilapidated rooms. They have cleared one plot of field and harvested half a load of grain.
There is always more than enough when boiling congee, yet there is never enough when preparing rice. This too surpasses those who seek fame, rushing south and then running north.
A verse in praise shown to the assembly.
When will this discourse on "is" and "is not" ever end? The ocean of ignorance is vast, and my mountain of ego is high.

If you have not yet purified the three delusions through the cultivation of the body, you must extinguish every single trace of them in all matters. Otherwise, your leisure and stillness will pass in vain; how can you digest the ready-made rice and gruel?
I speak these words with earnestness to all you practitioners of Chan: do not trade your *kāṣāya* robe for feathers.
Seeing off the Abbot of Donglin Temple as he returns to Huating to practice Chan:
A practitioner must be fierce and resolute. Like a hair-piercing sword, it is white as snow. Whether Buddha comes or Patriarch comes, seize it up and cut them down at once.
The wooden horse in the clouds neighs in alarm; the carp on the mountain bleeds. At the edge of the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, the victory is proclaimed.
Return! In the ordinary course of things, you have already trodden through the moonlight of Huating.
Send the attendant Qing back to his hometown to visit his teacher;
your teacher is advanced in years at Zhongshan Temple, and morning and evening there is no one to attend to him. Do not return to sweep the floors or carry the handkerchief for me.
"Vase. Is the ritual between teacher and disciple complete? Your mother is moreover advanced in years; with you as her only child, she has no other.
Her hopes are severed by the autumn wind, and she has not yet seen your return. Day after day she leans upon the gate, shedding tears incessantly.

Having left your teacher and abandoned your mother to enter the mountains, what purpose have you ultimately achieved? To find contentment in poverty and delight in the Way is indeed difficult. Yet here you dwell in this thatched hut..."
Building a hermitage is no easy matter. One must plant bamboos and pine trees; one must hoe the mountains and dig the earth; one must transport water and carry firewood;
one must irrigate vegetables and water taro tubers; one must practice the Way and recite the sutras; and one must restrain the mind and eliminate drowsiness.
Braggwort soup and millet rice to stanch the wounds of hunger; plain mustard greens and thin gruel to pass through the intestines and stomach.

All people in life are busy for the sake of their mouths and bodies; I, too, cannot escape the burden of this physical form. If one’s own mind-ground is not yet clear, the karmic consciousness remains vast and boundless, lacking any foundation.
Whether by the water or beneath the trees, we merely pass through briefly; neither you nor I have any plan to dwell here long-term. —Master Yuejiang.
A letter has arrived. There is a profound meaning in my exhortation for you to return. You opened the seal and withdrew before reading it;
thus you have not failed the message sent, fully embodying filial piety and righteousness. It is said that filial piety is the foremost of all virtues; whether layperson or monk, who does not agree?

Serving one’s teacher and honoring one’s mother is known as the "Field of Reverence. Why must you enter the assembly and practice Zen meditation? Suddenly longing for stillness, yet again finding clamor distasteful—this is shortsightedness.
Che does not hinder your coming and going at leisure.
Haedu-sa, seek my words and apply yourself with urgency to your practice. Hold up the "Wu" (No) of the Dog alone; keep your backbone erect and firm like Mount Sumeru.
Turn it over and examine it again and again; you must resolve this public case. If a fleeting delusive thought arises, you will immediately be driven about by it.
If you are diligent and never indolent, you may wait for the Way while sitting or standing. But if you are lazy and dull-witted, it will not happen even in a donkey’s lifetime.
If you can let go, there is nothing that can be done and nothing that cannot be done; the seventeen hundred "tangled vines" are all merely door-knocking tiles.
To Master Jin-an and Chan practitioner Jin of Danyang:
You have lived with me for some time. Although you have resolved to practice Zen, you have not yet attained any entry into it.
Regarding all the affairs within the hermitage, he never shrank from labor; his mouth and body were content with the simple and thin, and his mind and person were quite sincere.
One day he came before me and requested words to serve as a rule for the Dharma. I have written these few words to assist you in the power of advancing on the Path.
I shall simply dwell in my mountain retreat, passing day and night according to conditions. Do not emulate those wandering monks who travel east, west, south, and north.
Amidst your ordinary activities, be diligent and do not be lax. Raise your eyebrows and look: what, after all, is this?
When the one who looks through it is seen through, the great matter is finally brought to completion.

To show Layman Liu Tiebi that seeing one's nature and becoming a Buddha is no different from being a Buddha—ancient words are most straightforward; they cut off [delusion] right at the head, leaving not even a thread of doubt.
A hair’s breadth—by all means, do not seek it by following another’s words. Even if there are hundreds or thousands of kinds of falsehoods, in the end they all return to that one reality.
This old monk reveals his true heart, entrusting it to Liu Tiebi of the Cloudy Peaks.
The Four Postures in the Mountains:
Walking in the mountains, strolling with a leisurely gait, I climb the creepers and ascend another steep crag.
Dwelling in the mountains, through many mornings and evenings, I plant pine trees by hand until they grow into great, cool-shaded trees.
Sitting in the mountains, yellow leaves fall fluttering down. No one comes; I close the door and kindle a blazing fire.
Lying in the mountains, the pine wind passes through my ears. No reason for it; my good dreams are all blown away.
Beneath ten layers of steep cliffs, fire is used for seeds and the blade for plowing.
There is millet and vegetables; they may be boiled or stewed, sufficient to satisfy one's immediate needs.
I delight in my future lives; sitting here, I gaze at the branches of the courtyard trees. Through how many cycles of decay and flourishing have they passed?

Beneath these layered cliffs, I take the ancients as my peers. Having thoroughly realized the fundamental root, once it is understood, one simply rests. How bustling the assembly of seekers of the profound!
Contemplating the *huatou* of death is like waiting for a rabbit while guarding a tree stump, or marking the boat with a cut to search for a lost sword.
Beneath the deep crags, weeds and brush interlace daily; no human figure approaches. Yellow leaves drift and fall; valley birds cry out at twilight.
The mountain moon rises high at night; as the pine trees glisten with dew, cranes take flight, moistening my meditation robe.
Beneath the layered cliffs, snakes and tigers are my neighbors; yet since I have forgotten myself, their nature has also become tame. Such is the life of man in this world.
Each possesses innate purity. Bearing teeth and wearing hair, why do you act so unkindly?

Beneath the deep crags, you have not yet penetrated the fundamental root; when encountering objects and meeting conditions, you are tossed about in confusion. You must awaken to the underlying principle.
Transcending seeing and hearing, after a long time, one naturally encounters the source at every turn.
Dwelling in silent stillness beneath the layered crags, the three periods of time do not arrive; the mind is like a mirror, like a reflection. A slanting moon shines through half the window.
A single brazier of embers remains; alas for that sleeping man! His butterfly-dreams flutter on and on.
Beneath the layered crags stands a white-haired old man: his upper garment is boundless, his trousers have no opening. He enters into *dhyāna* at night.
By day I toil diligently in the fields and furrows; the Way lies therein—what else could there be?
Beneath the layered crags, my eyes face a thousand mountains. When the single root returns to its source, all six sense-bases become tranquil. White clouds drift and float.
The green waters murmur and flow; movement and stillness are naturally forgotten. This is truly another realm within the human world.
Beneath the layered cliffs, they do not cultivate their physical forms; they eat wood and wear grass, with cloth socks and bamboo shoes. Dense bamboo screens the dark windows.
Moss grows thick, covering the steps; in this desolation, one forgets worldly attachments. In silent stillness, the mind is empty and open.
Beneath the layered cliffs, one eats to full satisfaction and sleeps soundly. Indulging in such unrestrained ease, the years pass in vain. Now that old age and illness approach, [what can be done?]
All manner of sufferings press upon one another; like digging a well when already thirsty, one’s distress is in vain.
In this rhyme, I send off West Hall Master Zhi back to Lingyin:
We shared a single mat at the Jiangu Hall, Facing incense burners, we sat until sleep was forgotten. In the mountains and forests, there is no distinction between ritual and music, past and present.

In the past, the conditions of time and season have undergone change: the shadows of trees rise and fall beneath the deep-night moon; the cries of monkeys are long and short across the fifth-watch sky.
Having failed to receive news of the plum blossoms for two winters, I have once again made an appointment with them at Cold Spring.
At the time of Zhao Chuxin, the Elder Administrator, his strength failed him in old age;
unable to bear the weight of his shoes, he walked with a bamboo staff as his steps fell among the flowers. He waited for the moon and slept beside the clouds upon mossy rocks;
he sought plum blossoms and accompanied guests to their neighbors’ homes. Fragrant gruel from mountain fields was served in earthen bowls; snow floated upon the porcelain cups of water.
Grinding tea. Today, for my old father’s sake, I have gone out for a time; this mind has long remained amidst the mists and clouds.

Having bid farewell to the study-room of Nan-shan, I borrowed a dwelling by the clouds and lived there for two years. On clear days, when there was nothing to do, I would take my hoe along; with incense-fragrance, I gathered [herbs] from the neighbor's house.

Chrysanthemums: Gathering them while tender, I bring them back to plant my vegetables. When the autumn palace is silent, the mountain chimes have ceased; where the night window is empty, the cypress incense smoke is thin.
Tomorrow morning I shall depart again for other mountains; when will I return once more to read the Buddhist scriptures?

On an autumn day, along the road through Qin River, everywhere the west wind causes leaves to fall repeatedly. Having happened upon a lake temple, I find temporary refuge for my body. Of old friends, how many remain?
Of worldly affairs, ten thousand things, not one is true. The restless toil of life is all a dream; the manifest karmic retribution of each person—each is distinct.
Through this cause, others who understand this principle can dispel [such doubts]; they will never follow others and thereby harm their own spirits.
Having reached seventy-seven this year, my vitality has silently faded and old age and illness have increased. Treading through the snow to seek plum blossoms, one knows how to walk with care.
Heavy; as I pick through the clouds over the ridges, my shoulders ache. Time passes by as swiftly as a flying arrow. Worldly thoughts have faded away, cold as ice.
Yet I recall my former wanderings through mountain caves, when two or three times I ascended to the highest peak.
Last night was the winter solstice; the first yang has arisen. All things rejoice and turn toward glory. Iron trees bloom with clusters of red flowers;
stony fields produce green shoots of bamboo sprouts. In the human world, the days of transformation have gained but a thread’s length; beyond the bamboo, the secluded birds [begin their song].
Changing the tone: An old monk with white hair sits beneath the window; by the incense burner, he recites two lines of scripture many times over.

Yet, when summoned again by the Commissioner of Nanzhou, he sighs at being bound by karma in this Sahā world. Each time he reflects, he lets out a sigh of lamentation; in this world, one encounters many faces.
Tiger. Rarely have I seen a Buddha-mind snake within the mountains. To ward off the cold, I patch my robes with lotus leaves; to dispel drowsiness, I brew tea with blossoms from the waterfall.
Old and clumsy, I am weary of responding to the times; unable to obey your command, I shall remain amidst the mists and clouds.

Showing the Disciples in the Snow: Six petals drift and fall as night deepens; they sprinkle the windows like moths rushing at the lamp. For the mountain dweller, there is the wealth of a thousand trees of silver;
for the fisherman, the elegance of a single robe of jade. In the deep paths, the sound of woodcutters is utterly absent; yet on the shaded cliffs, there are hunters.
The person has passed. Before the hermitage, there is no place to find the yellow tubers; one sees only a few blossoms on the cold plum trees.
To the attendant Gao: you have attained Zen. You are worthy of ten thousand taels of gold. Is there not anyone in this world who can travel a thousand *li*?
A horse—humanity finds it difficult to find one such as Jiu Fang Gao.
Inside the lacquer workshop, he exhausts himself with ash; only then can he polish the exterior well. Although the numinous light is inherently present, [it must be refined].
To be present, one must also apply diligent effort to bring it forth.
When the Abbot Zhen was sent to pay homage at Yungwang,
Yan’gang, Tiantai, and Huading Peak, and when Nushan Lubao received him at Tiantong, he traveled everywhere yet never departed from the Two Peaks.
It is sufficient. Everything is contained within a single point of the mani-jewel.

As for sending [this] to Zen Master Jiu—who possesses the golden bones of every patriarch—why must one go to various places to pay homage at pagodas? How laughable that Dan Yang went to see Zen Master Jiu!
In the depths of spring, he traveled from Zhejiang to the east.

He saw off the Venerable Shen of Songjiang as he departed to visit various quarters and pay homage to the Patriarchs. As for external matters, a single application of effort lies within one's own person; to personally attend upon the Master, autumn has already arrived.
Half the year has passed; the trees are withered and leaves have fallen, revealing the golden wind.

As I see Master Chun depart to pay homage at Putuo, the cold tides roar day and night like the sound of thunder. Is listening with the ears not as intimate as listening with the eyes? Behold the White Flower Cliff for yourself.
Within the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, his entire body is manifested.

To the eminent Chan practitioner, he shows that from ancient times to the present, there is no dharma to be transmitted. One need only let the "thieving mind" die and then rest. For the most part, it is simply the self of others.
Agreed. Fuyuan would not force a bull’s head.
He sent Xuefeng, the *vina*, into the Incense Hall to chant the Buddha’s name ten times, startling Jiangxi’s Ma Boji. Eighty-four men could not support him.
Arise! The *vinaya-dhara* returns; do not let him be late.
Sending someone to travel to Wutai—go, go to the highest peak of Mount Tai! Mañjuśrī meets them with palms joined and a smile. Before the cliffs stands a golden lion.
Son, you ride backward on your horse to return to this old monk;

I send you off as a needle-worker, carrying scissors and a ruler as you travel to all quarters. The thread goes out and the needle comes back, day after day in a busy whirl. You measure the length and breadth of others until there is none left.
Short. How many times has one ever measured the length of one’s own home?
To the Venerable Zhen, the Head Seat, during the hundred-day period of the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) retreat, he urged him on with a sharp whip.
When one's effort reaches its full extent, the pivot of the teaching becomes perfect, and the karmic obstructions of many lifetimes are all extinguished.
Extinction. The realm of the Buddha is vividly present before one's eyes.
Sending off Real, the Chief Administrator, back to Dajue:
the skeletal frame and vital energy of Yangqi are majestic and powerful. For an entire summer, we have forgotten each other amidst the silence; now that autumn arrives, I long to return to Tianmu.
Departing, he quietly closed the bamboo hut to listen to the pines in the wind.
As he saw Monk Chian returning to his hometown, [the master asked]:
"For what reason do you travel alone on pilgrimage? What haste is there in taking up your staff to return home? If one does not cultivate pure deeds nor practice meditation...
Meeting. Alas, how lamentable it is that such precious time has passed in vain.
De-du Sŏsa returns to his home village;
De-un is not on Mount Myohyang, but shall come to meet me on another mountain. From this day forth, I shall cease my travels.
Mindfulness: Sitting and watching the ground of the mind, the flowers of awakening bloom.

For many years, Attendant Zhen has been among the assembly to practice Chan; though he was called three times, the karmic conditions have not yet reached their limit. Go once more to various quarters to seek further invitations.
Yi, come here and receive this coarse blow!
To escort Master Fú and pay homage to the ancestral patriarchs' stupas is like a brick from Húlún;
they are found only by the mountains and by the waters. One must circumambulate and pay reverence to each one from beginning to end.
All-pervasive. The straw sandals remain as they were; he returns the money himself. To the visiting monk:
when will looking at the water and looking at the mountains ever end? When will this running south and rushing north ever cease? Piteous indeed is one whose body is clad in the *kāṣāya*.
Down. Before the path of practice is completed, one’s hair has already turned white.
Two verses on sending off a barber who waits for an imperial summons to cultivate karmic affinity:

When the barber who waits for an imperial summons arrived at the mountain, all the monks in the corridors straightened their appearance. Why does the old man in the abbot’s quarters not [do the same]?
Shaving. One must leave one's white hair until past the deep winter.
Shaving again as it grows, and growing again after shaving—how many times in a year this distant trouble exceeds! The Great Physician simply comes to seek [the patient].
"Fortune! How much fortune do I possess?

I have sent the venerable Master Yuan to manifest his entire being in wondrous purity and perfect clarity. There is no need to come and ask me how it is. This is precisely for the sake of the traveling Zen practitioners."
My son, how much understanding have you ever truly possessed?

I shall send this question back to the Master, who will clearly speak a single phrase of the Great Vehicle to you: "Cold as a fierce fire, hot as ice. If the Master does not believe me, [then let him verify it].
He spoke thus: "Hurry back at once and inquire about the Mahāyāna.
With a short staff and a light pack, he set out for Mount Wutai to see off his companion. The main gates of the Silver Towers and Golden Pavilions opened; there he met Mañjuśrī and partook of tea.
It is finished. Bring the glass cups here.
Send the guest monk to stay in the Mahāyāna Hall during the summer. When he first came to knock at the gate of Fuyuan in the winter, do not resent me, an old man, for having nothing to say.
It is said: "A single verse of a fisherman’s song is heard from across the shore.

For one who sends off a seeker of the Way, if one's effort does not reach its limit, it will not be square or round. When the mind is firm, even stone is pierced. Have you not seen the old dhūta monk Kāśyapa?
Leaves. The faculty of mind is extinguished as he receives the golden robe;

he is sent to the great *venerable* (vinaya-master) to examine the place where the mother’s bucket handle exploded, thereby seeing the root source. Re-traversing the familiar path for three months of heaven, the sun warms the *xuancao* (daylily) in the northern hall.
Lü: "Do not speak of 'the wife’s Chan' to your mother.

To Master Mào, I show that becoming a Buddha or being reborn in heaven is an easy matter; the most difficult thing of all is to be a *dhūta*. To labor until the body is but dry bone—this is true tranquility."
There were few [monks]. Water was carried and firewood was hauled by everyone on general duty.
A man of the Way, having sought me out from afar, arrived at鹅湖 (Ehu). He earnestly inquired about the practice of *gongfu*. This old monk truly acts for the sake of others.
It is said: "Not a single word of the verses on origins remains.
Send forth diligent effort;
seek out the admonitions with diligence to practice the *gongfu*. Scatter and eliminate all distraction and dullness. Then, in the late night, the black clouds will dissipate.
Exhausted. The vast sky is like water, the moon’s orb solitary.
Two poems for Zen practitioners end here:
All day long you ride the ox, yet you do not know the ox. Why must you toil so hard seeking it elsewhere? It takes nothing more than to pull it by the nose and lead it back.
Look! This is simply this very ordinary head.
Once you have penetrated Vzhou’s “Mu” (No), the mysterious pass and golden locks are all opened through. At the third watch under the moon, the earthen ox bellows;
on all eight sides, the sea-sun is bright and radiant.
