Seeking words from Master Ying, a guest braved the spring chill to visit his secluded gate. His patched robe still clings to light flakes of snow. Having sat for a while, he presented me with the sayings of various quarters;
before the brocade scrolls were even unrolled, my eyes were already brightened.
As the Venerable One of Jiangxi departs for the West, his noble ambition has led him out from the monastic groves. A single inch of time is a single inch of gold;
do not casually bury the heart of the Patriarch with worldly, idle learning.
Seeing off Attendant Ling on his return to Jingci:
Ten li of lake light drenches the six bridges. When you arrive, you must keep your eyes open and your head high. The wind is warm along the broken embankment as willow blossoms fall;
It is not the bird’s nest blowing away the monk’s robe-hair.

Sent to Attendant Guan to let go of body and mind and return to self-observation: there is not even a hair’s breadth of deception here. When clouds gather and mists roll away, heaven and earth are vast;
as the moon rises over the green mountains, it is a single sphere of jade.
To show the Way to Le Dao:
it is a patch of fallow field and a single hoe. Turn it over and over again with diligent effort;
when one stroke of the hoe turns the spring breeze, there will be melons and eggplants, and there will also be gourds.
I show the assembly:
even before a thought has arisen, there is still deluded awareness; the moment a single thought flickers into being, one harms others. When your practice reaches this point, you must take heed:
before the withered tree at the crag, many stray from the path.
The one who shows the Way has traveled to the ends of the lands in the east, west, south, and north; now that he is able to bring this mind to rest, Jueyi remains dwelling only in the mountains,
enjoying the single finger-tip of the devas and nāgas.
The Dharma Master Bānjiè, with blood from his own head, transcribed the Lotus Sutra to repay his father.
Who was the father? Who was the mother? With five heinous crimes in his breast, he was a true son. Behold the place where righteousness cuts through and emotion is forgotten:
three or four branches of the lotus flower are in full bloom.
The Constant Attendant has transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in blood;
wherever this scripture resides, there is the Buddha. There is no need for further exertion of mind or strength. In the late autumn at Jetavana, the frost is heavy;
the tree leaves are redder than a deep dye of blood.
The monk who dwells in the city wall as a head scribe is rebuked by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; most of the ancient worthies were hidden away in mountain caves.
When mountain springs flow out into the human world, clear water naturally becomes turbid waves.
Entrusting myself to Master Pingshan of Jingci, I am old in years and solitary at heart, longing for my brothers. At Mount Zhongfeng, I rejoice that you have passed through Nanping.
The gurgling flow of the twin streams—how much more pleasant it is to hear as they enter West Lake!
With broken hooves and pierced noses, five hundred oxen are gathered into a single pen within Nanping Temple. Their hides and fur have been restored to a lustrous sheen;
they pull the plow and drag the harrow once more, raising their heads.

Two Poems Sent to a Friend In my mountain cottage, weary and listless, I lie late at night; Because of you, I am made to remember last year’s time. Beneath the bean-vine trellis, we once shared a single mat;
When the moon sank behind the pine needles, we still chanted our poems.
A three-bay cottage within the shadows of Ten-Thousand-Pine; a single monk before a cliff of withered wood.
Passing twenty or thirty years in this manner—would you ever trade such pure simplicity for empty fame?
Presented to Guqiao:
Before the empty kalpa, there was a shadowless tree; it supports the heavens and props up the earth, its bare branches stark and clear.
From Xinzhou comes a wood-seller who gathers them up and carries them away on a single shoulder.
Presented to Wukan:
Raising my head and gazing in the four directions, all is a vast expanse of white. North, south, east, and west—none can be discerned. There is no need for an oar to push to the bottom;
turning one’s head is the very moment to board the boat.

Bestowed upon the source, it flows forth from within the heart-mind in surging waves. Lowering itself as circumstances require, it does not exalt itself; halting at the pit or flowing onward are but secondary matters.
In the end, it returns to the great ocean to become the surging tides.
Presented to Shiya:
A thousand fathoms rising from the earth, green as jade; ten thousand feet soaring above the clouds, hard as steel. Beholding such perilous precipices, many retreat;
who is there willing to let go of all and take it up?

Bestowed with the peerless eye, his spirit fills the lakes and seas and towers above the clouds. Outstanding among the monastic community, his thoughts are beyond compare. From antiquity to the present, who is my equal?
Where you can afford to be generous, be generous.
Presented to Baitan:
A single color, empty and luminous, contains the entire Dharma-realm; its four eaves are as pure and bright as ice and frost.
Through several snow-clear nights at the small window, though no plum blossoms are seen, one only perceives their fragrance.
Parting Gift for Jian Zhanran:
Not entering the ranks of the common stream, he stares with fixed eyes; when the fruit of his coming is realized, it will surely be extraordinary.
If one can simply brew tea to enhance its fine flavor, who could allow themselves to drift aimlessly across rivers and lakes?
Parting Gift:
The peaks are steep and lofty; ten thousand peaks cannot rival them. Solitary and precarious, the majesty of the myriad mountains is difficult to equal.
Where Sudhana found the place of the clouds, it lay further beyond that verdant expanse.
True Praise of the Buddha Emerging from the Mountains, Two Poems:
With disheveled hair descending through the emerald peaks, Frosty clouds and lingering snow cling to his *kāṣāya*. There is no need to further inquire of the matters within the mountains;
By beholding his countenance, one shall know them at once.
Elbows broken, robes tattered, bones wrapped in skin; descending the mountain, he turns his head, his steps slow and weary. O Father King, do not send men to inquire after him;
his appearance is no longer like it was within the palace.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, you two youths who have gone south in search of the Way have not yet returned; I have gazed toward the White Flower Cliff for a long time.
On a night when ten thousand *li* of the vast sky are cloudless, the moon speaks from the heart of the waves—to whom can it speak?
Water is itself the wave; a cliff is itself the rock. To sit and realize perfect penetration is the foremost way.
The two-headed Arhat does nothing at all;
he sits in meditation for long years, clinging to the dharma and practicing asceticism like an ox pulling a millstone, until quiescence manifests before him.
He did not see what was before him; he waited for the master to emerge from samādhi to re-examine it.
With one entire body and a single flask of autumn water, such is his life beyond the mundane world—this alone is it.
With a white-eyed glance, he looks upon the people of this world, merely smiling as he presses his hands against his crossed legs.
Bodhidharma had two heads and a black face;
his teeth were missing and his mind was coarse and bold. On the dais of the Liang Emperor, he scattered sand and flung earth;
before the peak of Shaoshi, he blossomed and bore fruit. At the rock terrace of the oak-leaf cave, he sat in meditative repose with his head shrouded. This is what is called Bodhidharma.
A single word did not accord, so he crossed the Yangtze and Huai rivers; at Mount Xionger, he went to be buried alive. His boundless worldly possessions were all scattered in ruin;
what need was there to quarrel over a single pair of worn-out leather shoes?
Regarding the two elder bhikṣus, Master Zan and Master An, depicted together in the same portrait:
what was the cause for this? When they first met in Jianyang Mountain—one awakened first, the other awakened later—they were as affectionate as bone and flesh;
yet after their second meeting at Xifeng Temple, they became as hostile as bitter enemies. From that point on...
The father faces south and the son faces north; unaware that clouds disperse and waters flow away. For you, the retribution is exhausted and you have returned to Tuṣita;
for me, karmic afflictions still linger in Jambudvīpa. Where right and wrong, or gratitude and resentment, are difficult to distinguish—a single patch of pine shade covers a stone.
He praises himself, saying:
"The teeth on my wooden board grow hair; my face is devoid of flesh. Having received the prediction upon Mount Ling, I lack the blessings of devas and humans.
Lean and angular, I am like a jade crag surging from the heart of the blue ocean waves; hard and bare, I resemble a peak rising amidst a mass of white clouds."
Protruding from the thousand-fathom stone house, some say it is the Master of Tianhu Hermitage, yet he is not of my own kindred;
others call him the Abbot of Fuyuan, yet he is likewise not among my followers. Those who lack the sinews within their eyes cannot help but engage in wild conjecture upon mere shadows;
those who possess blood beneath their skin will never engage in idle divination based on painted images. *Ei!*
By all means, do not display it for others to see. Hang it in a quiet room to keep company with the pines and bamboos.
This Chan practitioner seeks praise;
his hair is white and his face is wrinkled, his skin is yellowed and his bones are emaciated. He has exhausted his own mind and laughed the mouths of others to pieces. I know this well.
In this degenerate age, the Way is difficult to practice; thus I have come to a quiet place to sit idly with hands folded.

I watch as the waters of Tianhu and Gehu flow together, and face the twin peaks of Xiafeng and Xufeng, both mountains equally beautiful. By what cause can one attain such leisure? It is truly because one is able to leap through and penetrate [the truth].
This is not for me, a Chan elder, to boast of myself; throughout ancient and modern times, it has been said that Suzhou possesses it.
Verse on Departing from the World:
The green mountains do not harbor stinking corpses; once dead, what need is there to dig a pit and bury? Look at me:
I have no samādhi-fire; I am but a pile of firewood that has outshone the past and cut off the future.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Shiwu, Volume Lower (End).
Epitaph for the Stupa of Chan Master Fuyuan Shiwu Yong,
composed by the Śramaṇa Yuanxu of the former Yanshou Chan Monastery in Siming.
The Master’s name was Qinggong; his style name was Shiwu. He was a native of Changshu in Suzhou. His secular surname was Wen, and his mother was Lady Liu.
On the night of his birth, there was an extraordinary light; this was indeed the eighth year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty, the *renshen* year.

Upon reaching adulthood, he relied upon the monk Yongwei of Xingjiao Chongfu Temple in his home prefecture to leave the household life. At twenty, he shaved his head; three years later, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). One day...
A monk carrying a staff and a bamboo hat passed by the gate. The Master questioned him, and the monk said, "I am now heading to Tianmu to see Master Gaofeng.
Would you care to accompany me? The Master joyfully went with him to see Feng. Feng asked, "For what purpose have you come? The Master replied, "I wish to seek the Great Dharma.
Feng said, "Is the Great Dharma so easily sought? You must burn off a finger as incense [as an offering]."
The Master said, "Today I have personally seen the Abbot; how could the Great Dharma have any secrets?
Feng silently took him as a worthy vessel and bestowed upon him the phrase, "The myriad dharmas return to One. He served diligently for three years, yet the Great Matter remained unclarified.
Suddenly, he took leave to travel elsewhere. Feng said, "In Wenzhou there is the Blind Donkey; in Huai, there is Ji’an. You should go to see them. He arrived at Xifeng in Jianyang and met Ji’an.
Yun’an asked, “Where have you come from? The Master said, “From Tianmu. Yun’an asked, “What instruction did he give you?
The Master said, “All phenomena return to the One. Yun’an asked, “How do you understand this? The Master was speechless. Yun’an said, “This is a dead word.
What kind of person suffering from a feverish illness would teach you such a thing? The Master bowed and requested further guidance. Yun’an said, “Do not dwell where there is a Buddha.”
"When there is no Buddha, run past quickly. "What is the meaning of this? The Master answered, but it did not accord with the Abbot's intent.

The Abbot said, "This too is a dead word. The Master was suddenly overcome with perspiration. Later, when he entered the room for private instruction, the Abbot again took up the previous conversation to interrogate him.

The Master replied, "One sees the road while mounting the horse. The Abbot rebuked him, saying, "Having stayed here for six years, you still hold such a view! The Master was filled with indignation and abandoned [his practice].
On his way out, he suddenly raised his head and saw a pavilion in the breeze; he attained sudden enlightenment.
Returning, he said to the Abbot, "To not dwell where there is a Buddha is a dead word; to hurry past where there is no Buddha is also a dead word.
Today I have realized the living word. The Abbot asked, "How do you understand it? The Master replied, "Rain on the Qingming festival."
The weather had just cleared. A yellow oriole sang clearly from atop a branch. Yun’an nodded his head in approval. After a long while, the bird took its leave.

As Yun’an saw him out the door, he instructed him, saying, "In the future, you shall share the same shrine with me. Not long after, Yun’an moved to Daochang on Lake Dongting. The Master went there to pay his respects again.
Subsequently, Yun’an appointed him to manage the treasury keys. Yun’an once remarked to the assembly, "This man is a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net in the ocean of the Dharma."
The entire assembly watched with bated breath. Later, Master Yintang Yin of Lingyin Monastery occupied the second seat in the assembly and subsequently ceased formal study.

He ascended Mount Xiawu and established a hermitage named Tianhu. His Way was harmonized with both the monastic and the lay, and visitors arrived in such numbers that their shoes were piled at the door.

Whatever was required for the ritual feasts of the first and last months of the year came to him spontaneously without being sought. As for the labor of gathering firewood and vegetables, he performed it all with his own hands. There was...
The style of the ancient worthies was such that, in their leisure from meditation, they delighted in composing mountain retreat poems, many of which have been passed down.
The Master harbored the intention to spend his final days on this mountain. Shortly thereafter, the newly established Fuyuan Chan monastery in Danghu, Jiahe, heard of the Master’s reputation;
the Guangjiao Monastery dispatched an official summons to earnestly invite him to serve as its second-generation abbot. The Master remained firmly reclining and would not rise, yet...
Someone exhorted him, saying, "A śramaṇa ought to take the propagation of the Dharma as his primary responsibility.
To dwell in seclusion and pursue solitary excellence—how can that be considered sufficient? Thereupon, he rose up resolutely and opened wide the forge, refining those who studied under him.
Contemporaries remarked that he was truly one capable of reviving the tradition of the Jia-an school. After seven years, he retired on account of old age and returned once more to Tian.
Lake [Monastery]. During the Zhizheng era, the imperial court heard of the Master’s reputation and sent down incense and silk offerings to honor his extraordinary virtue.
The Empress bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered robe, which all people considered a great honor; yet the Master remained as serene and unassuming as ever.

On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the autumn of the Renchen year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. Two days later, at midnight, he took leave of the assembly. His disciples requested, saying, "After the Master passes away..."
"What shall be done? he asked. He then took up his brush and wrote a verse: "The green mountains do not harbor a stinking corpse;
Once dead, why need one dig a pit to bury it? I, too, lack the fire of samādhi; A single pile of firewood, cutting off the past and ending the future. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
When his body was cremated, relics of five colors shone brilliantly, their number beyond counting. His disciples collected his sacred remains and enshrined them.
The stupa was erected on the plain of Tianhu, together with the stupa of his meditation hut, to demonstrate that he did not forget the master’s intention of sharing the same niche.
He lived to the age of eighty-one and had been a monk for fifty-four years. Among his disciples was one named Yutagu.
He was a native of Goryeo who personally received the Master’s instructions and was confirmed by means of a verse, which contained the line: "There is a golden scale upon the straight hook.

His King honored him with the title of National Preceptor (Guksa). Having heard of the Master's spiritual practice, the King’s mind was deeply moved and filled with longing; he sent an envoy to express his devotion.
The Imperial Court issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Chan Master Foci Huizhao.

An official communication was sent to Jiangzhe, requesting that Master Pingshan Lin of Jingci Temple personally enter Tianhu to collect the master’s *śarīra* (relics) and escort them back to the country. Pingshan had been a fellow practitioner (*tongcan*) with the master.

All of this accords with Master Yong’s original intent. His formal discourses from the high seat (*shàngtáng fǎyǔ*) and his mountain-dwelling poems and verses were compiled by his disciples, who were exceedingly gentle, and have been published for the world.
Furthermore, they requested that I compose an inscription based on the Master’s biographical sketch (*xíngzhuàng*). I previously met the Master at Fuyuan;
his form was emaciated, yet the resonance of the Way (*dàoyùn*) was overflowing. It has now been more than forty years since then, which moves me to deep reflection.
He composed an inscription for it. The inscription reads:
The direct pointing from the West, A separate transmission outside the teachings— Only those of the highest capacity Are able to attain it.
The transmission is without transmission; Attainment is without attainment. Like the great void, It is vast and boundless.
In a stone hut, volume after volume; his mind like extinguished ashes. Suddenly, with a flash, he attained awakening—a lotus blooming amidst the flames.
Grandson of Huairang, son of Wuzhun. From a pure source flows a long stream; with flourishing roots, the fruit is surely realized.
His traces remain at Xiawu; his fame falls upon the lakes and rivers. People vie to be the first to behold him, like the auspicious star or the phoenix.
From the time of his entry into parinirvāṇa until now, nearly thirty years have passed; the twin pagodas stand loftily, and the pure breeze has not ceased.
